The patient is a 37-year-old woman with a history of a resected left perineal schwannoma (with local recurrence) who now presents with multiple homogeneously enhancing, bead-like intradural/intraspinal lesions in the lumbosacral vertebral canal (L1–S1), histologically confirmed as schwannomas. The presence of multiple pathologically proven schwannomas involving both spinal nerve roots and peripheral nerves without vestibular schwannomas (normal head imaging) and without an NF2 mutation rules out neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2-related schwannomatosis) and meets the clinical diagnostic criteria for schwannomatosis. Because genetic testing is negative for NF2, SMARCB1, and LZTR1 mutations and the family history is negative, this represents sporadic (or non-NF2/NOS) schwannomatosis.
Final diagnosis: Schwannomatosis (sporadic schwannomatosis)

Multiple bead-like intradural nodules from L1 to S1, homogeneously enhancing, with no cyst, hemorrhage or necrosis. This pattern suggests multiple benign nerve sheath tumors.
A prior perineal schwannoma was resected, a mobile perineal nodule has now recurred, and the canal lesions are pathology-confirmed schwannoma. That makes at least two non-intradermal schwannomas in separate locations.
Head, cervical and thoracic imaging is normal, so there are no vestibular schwannomas or meningiomas, which argues against NF2.
Germline testing is negative for NF2, SMARCB1 and LZTR1, and there is no family history.
There is no neurological deficit. Chronic constipation may be a mild cauda equina effect.
Schwannomatosis (genetically unexplained, "not elsewhere classified")
NF2-related schwannomatosis (mosaic)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 with multiple spinal neurofibromas
Myxopapillary ependymoma with CSF seeding
Leptomeningeal metastases or drop metastases
Schwannomatosis.
For: multiple pathology-proven schwannomas in separate sites, spinal and peripheral predominance, no vestibular tumors, no neurological deficit.
Against: no pathogenic variant was found, but that is expected in this category.
Mosaic NF2.
For: blood testing can miss mosaic NF2; multiple schwannomas.
Against: normal head imaging with no vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas or ependymomas.
NF1 neurofibromas.
For: multiple spinal nerve sheath tumors.
Against: histology is schwannoma, and there are no café-au-lait macules or other NF1 stigmata.
Myxopapillary ependymoma with seeding.
For: lumbosacral intradural location.
Against: histology is schwannoma, and the rest of the neuraxis is normal.
Metastases.
For: multiple intradural nodules.
Against: no primary cancer, years of stability (2022 to 2024), benign pathology.
NF1, ependymoma and metastases are excluded by histology.
NF2 is unlikely because there are no cranial or vestibular lesions and germline NF2 testing is negative. Tumor-tissue NF2 analysis could still exclude mosaicism formally.
I commit to schwannomatosis because she has at least two pathologically confirmed non-intradermal schwannomas without vestibular schwannoma.
Final diagnosis: Schwannomatosis (no NF2, SMARCB1 or LZTR1 variant identified, i.e. schwannomatosis-NEC), with multiple lumbosacral intraspinal schwannomas and recurrent perineal schwannoma.

History of prior perineal schwannoma (2019) with palpable local recurrence: Demonstrates a predisposition to multiple peripheral nerve sheath tumors.
Multiple bead-like, well-defined, homogeneously enhancing nodules in the lumbosacral canal (L1–S1) on MRI (2022 and 2024): Classic imaging appearance of multiple intradural extramedullary cauda equina/lumbosacral nerve root tumors without necrosis or cystic degeneration.
Pathological confirmation of schwannoma (March 2024): Definitively establishes the histologic identity of the lumbosacral lesions.
Normal head, cervical, and thoracic spine imaging: Rules out bilateral vestibular schwannomas and other intracranial/higher spinal tumors.
Negative family history and negative genetic testing for NF2, SMARCB1, and LZTR1: Excludes NF2-related schwannomatosis and known germline SMARCB1/LZTR1-related forms, which is consistent with sporadic schwannomatosis (where a substantial proportion of cases lack detectable germline mutations in these genes).
Sporadic schwannomatosis
NF2-related schwannomatosis (Neurofibromatosis type 2)
Multiple spinal neurofibromas (Neurofibromatosis type 1)
Intradural extramedullary drop metastases (leptomeningeal carcinomatosis)
Myxopapillary ependymoma of the cauda equina
Sporadic schwannomatosis:
For: Pathologically confirmed schwannomas at multiple non-intradermal anatomical sites (lumbosacral vertebral canal and left perineum), absence of vestibular schwannomas on normal head MRI, negative NF2 genetic testing, and negative family history. Negative SMARCB1 and LZTR1 testing does not exclude sporadic schwannomatosis.
Against: No identified pathogenic germline variant in SMARCB1 or LZTR1 (though genetically uncharacterized sporadic cases are well-recognized).
NF2-related schwannomatosis (Neurofibromatosis type 2):
For: Multiple spinal schwannomas along the cauda equina.
Against: Normal head imaging (no vestibular schwannomas or meningiomas), negative NF2 genetic testing, and negative family history.
Multiple spinal neurofibromas (Neurofibromatosis type 1):
For: Multiple lumbosacral nerve root nodules and subcutaneous perineal nodules.
Against: Pathology definitively confirmed schwannoma rather than neurofibroma; negative family history and absence of other NF1 stigmata on physical examination.
Intradural extramedullary drop metastases:
For: Multiple bead-like enhancing nodules along the lumbosacral spinal canal/cauda equina.
Against: Indolent course (stable from 2022 to 2024 without neurological deficits), normal brain/cervical/thoracic imaging, and definitive pathology confirming benign schwannoma.
Myxopapillary ependymoma:
For: Common tumor of the lumbosacral canal/cauda equina in young adults.
Against: Typically solitary and often hemorrhagic or cystic; ruled out by pathology confirming schwannoma and by the concurrent perineal schwannoma.
NF2-related schwannomatosis is excluded by normal head imaging (absence of vestibular schwannomas) and negative NF2 genetic testing. Neurofibromatosis type 1, drop metastases, and myxopapillary ependymoma are definitively excluded by surgical histopathology confirming schwannoma. Given multiple anatomically distinct, histologically confirmed schwannomas (lumbosacral canal and perineum) without vestibular schwannomas or NF2 mutation, the diagnosis commits to sporadic schwannomatosis.
Final diagnosis: Sporadic schwannomatosis

A 37-year-old woman has multiple schwannomas: a previously resected left perineal schwannoma, a likely perineal recurrence, and multiple bead-like nodules from L1 to S1 in the lumbosacral canal, with resection pathology confirming schwannoma. Head imaging is normal, so there are no vestibular schwannomas. There is no family history of neurofibromatosis. Germline testing is negative for NF2, SMARCB1, and LZTR1. Multiple non-vestibular, non-intradermal schwannomas without vestibular tumors and without NF2 features fit schwannomatosis. The negative gene panel places it in the gene-negative category: schwannomatosis not otherwise specified, or possibly mosaic disease not detectable in blood.
Final diagnosis: Schwannomatosis (gene-negative / NOS, non-NF2-related), with multiple lumbosacral intraspinal schwannomas and a recurrent perineal schwannoma

The patient has synchronous bilateral poorly differentiated (G3) invasive ductal carcinomas. The left tumor is triple-negative with Ki-67 of 50%. After surgery she developed a spiculated lung nodule, adrenal and subcutaneous metastases, all CK7-positive. The lung biopsy showed carcinoma resembling the breast tumors. It was negative for TTF1 and napsin A, which argues against primary lung adenocarcinoma, and negative for p40, which argues against squamous carcinoma. The driver-mutation panel was entirely wild-type. GATA3 can be negative in triple-negative breast cancer. The family history (breast cancer in a paternal aunt) raises the possibility of a hereditary predisposition. Overall, the picture best fits metastatic disease from the triple-negative breast carcinoma.
Final diagnosis: Metastatic triple-negative breast carcinoma (from synchronous bilateral invasive ductal carcinoma) to the lung, adrenal gland and subcutaneous tissue

Synchronous bilateral breast carcinomas. Both are poorly differentiated (G3), node-negative, triple-negative, with Ki-67 of 50%.
After surgery there are new lung, adrenal and subcutaneous lesions.
The lung biopsy is morphologically similar to the breast tumors.
The lung tumor is CK7-positive and negative for TTF-1, napsin A and p40, which argues against primary lung adenocarcinoma and squamous carcinoma.
GATA3 is negative. This is a known pitfall, because GATA3 sensitivity is reduced in triple-negative breast cancer.
The lung tumor has no actionable lung driver alterations.
There is a strong family history of cancer, including breast cancer in a paternal aunt.
Metastatic triple-negative breast carcinoma (lung, adrenal, subcutaneous)
Primary TTF-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma, synchronous with the breast cancers
Metastatic carcinoma of another primary, such as upper GI or pancreaticobiliary
Primary lung squamous or large-cell carcinoma
Metastatic breast carcinoma.
For: known aggressive bilateral triple-negative disease, the same morphology in the lung, CK7 positivity, a lung marker profile that is negative.
Against: GATA3 negativity and node-negative primaries. Neither is unusual in triple-negative breast cancer.
Primary lung adenocarcinoma.
For: a spiculated lung nodule and a CK7-positive carcinoma.
Against: TTF-1 and napsin A are negative, there are no driver mutations, and the morphology mirrors the breast tumors.
Another primary.
For: CK7-positive carcinoma of unknown origin.
Against: no GI or pancreatic lesion is described, and the morphology resembles the breast tumors.
Lung squamous or large-cell carcinoma.
Against: p40 is negative and the morphology is not consistent.
Primary lung carcinoma is excluded by the immunoprofile (TTF-1, napsin A and p40 negative) and the absence of driver mutations.
Another primary is unsupported.
I commit to metastatic breast origin, based on matching morphology and the known high-grade triple-negative primaries. Germline testing (BRCA1/2 and similar) is warranted given the family history.
Final diagnosis: Metastatic triple-negative breast carcinoma (from synchronous bilateral invasive ductal carcinoma) to the lung, adrenal gland and subcutaneous tissue.

Bilateral poorly differentiated breast carcinomas (left IDC pT1c/G3/N0, right pT1b/G3/N0) that are triple-negative (ER/PR/HER2-negative) with high Ki-67 (50%): Establishes an aggressive, high-grade triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) phenotype capable of early hematogenous dissemination even without nodal involvement.
Post-surgery CT showing a spiculated pulmonary nodule, hypodense nodules, and adrenal metastasis: Indicates distant visceral metastatic disease, raising the critical question of metastatic TNBC versus a synchronous primary lung carcinoma.
Endoscopic lung biopsy showing carcinoma with histologic features similar to the breast neoplasms: Directly links the pulmonary lesion morphologically to the resected breast carcinomas.
Immunohistochemistry (CK7-positive; TTF-1, napsin A, P40, and GATA3-negative) and wild-type lung driver panel (ALK, EGFR, ROS1, RET, METex14, NTRK, BRAF): Argues strongly against primary lung adenocarcinoma (TTF-1/napsin A negative, no lung driver mutations) and squamous cell carcinoma (P40 negative), while remaining consistent with poorly differentiated TNBC (which is CK7-positive and frequently loses GATA3 expression).
Metastatic triple-negative breast carcinoma (pulmonary, adrenal, and subcutaneous metastases)
Primary TTF-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma (NSCLC) with bilateral breast and adrenal metastases
Synchronous primary poorly differentiated non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC-NOS)
Carcinoma of unknown primary (CUP)
Metastatic triple-negative breast carcinoma:
For: Known high-grade (G3, Ki-67 50%) ER/PR/HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma; lung biopsy shows carcinoma with features similar to the breast neoplasms; CK7-positive; negative lung lineage markers (TTF-1, napsin A, P40); wild-type for all tested lung adenocarcinoma driver mutations. Loss of GATA3 is common in poorly differentiated TNBC.
Against: Spiculated pulmonary nodule morphology and adrenal metastasis are classic for primary lung cancer; GATA3 is negative; breast tumors were small and node-negative (pT1c/N0 and pT1b/N0).
Primary TTF-1-negative lung adenocarcinoma with bilateral breast metastases:
For: Spiculated pulmonary nodule, adrenal metastasis, maternal history of lung cancer, bilateral small node-negative breast tumors (which can mimic metastases to the breast), and negative GATA3.
Against: Both TTF-1 and napsin A are negative; all 7 lung driver genes are wild-type; breast mastectomy specimens were formally diagnosed as invasive ductal carcinoma, and the lung biopsy was described as having features similar to the breast neoplasms.
Synchronous primary poorly differentiated NSCLC-NOS:
For: Spiculated lung lesion, adrenal metastasis, CK7 positivity, and negative GATA3.
Against: Histologic similarity between the lung biopsy and the breast neoplasms, negative TTF-1/napsin A/P40, and absence of lung driver mutations make a separate primary lung malignancy less likely than metastasis from the known high-grade TNBC.
Carcinoma of unknown primary (CUP):
For: Poorly differentiated CK7-positive carcinoma with negative organ-specific markers (TTF-1, napsin A, P40, GATA3) and inconclusive subcutaneous biopsy.
Against: A well-documented primary triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast is already established, and the lung biopsy matches its histologic features.
Primary squamous cell lung carcinoma is excluded by negative P40. Primary lung adenocarcinoma and NSCLC-NOS are argued against by negative TTF-1 and napsin A, wild-type status across all major lung driver genes, and the direct morphological similarity of the lung biopsy to the previously resected high-grade triple-negative breast carcinomas. Carcinoma of unknown primary is excluded because a known high-grade primary breast malignancy explains the histologic and immunophenotypic profile (CK7-positive, triple-negative, GATA3-negative). Therefore, the diagnosis commits to metastatic triple-negative breast carcinoma.
Final diagnosis: Metastatic triple-negative breast carcinoma (metastatic invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast)

The patient is a 64-year-old woman diagnosed with bilateral, poorly differentiated, triple-negative (ER-, PR-, HER2-) invasive ductal carcinomas of the breast (left pT1c/G3/N0, right pT1b/G3/N0) with a high Ki-67 index (50%). Postoperative CT revealed a spiculated pulmonary nodule, adrenal metastasis, and subcutaneous nodules. Biopsy of the lung lesion showed carcinoma with histological features similar to her breast neoplasms. Immunohistochemistry of the lung biopsy was CK7-positive and negative for all primary lung lineage markers (TTF-1 and Napsin A for lung adenocarcinoma; p40 for squamous cell carcinoma), and molecular testing was wild-type for all major non-small cell lung cancer oncogenic drivers (ALK, EGFR, ROS1, RET, METex14, NTRK, BRAF). Although GATA3 was negative, loss of GATA3 expression is common in high-grade triple-negative breast carcinomas. Together, the matching histomorphology, CK7-positive/TTF-1-negative/Napsin A-negative/p40-negative immunoprofile, and absence of lung driver mutations confirm pulmonary metastasis from her triple-negative breast cancer.
Final diagnosis: Metastatic triple-negative breast cancer

The patient is an asymptomatic 30-year-old primigravida presenting for routine antenatal care at 12 weeks of gestation. Ultrasound shows an empty endometrial cavity with a gestation located near the left uterine horn, and MRI confirms a live 12-week fetus (crown-rump length 5.8 cm) located within the left fallopian tube. Because the patient has no abdominal pain, tenderness, guarding, or hemodynamic instability, this represents an unruptured advanced first-trimester tubal (likely interstitial/cornual) ectopic pregnancy.
Final diagnosis: Unruptured ectopic pregnancy (left tubal/interstitial ectopic pregnancy)

An asymptomatic 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy was seen at routine 12-week booking. Ultrasound showed the gestation near the left uterine horn with an empty endometrial cavity. MRI confirmed a live 12-week fetus (CRL 5.8 cm) within the left fallopian tube. She has no signs of rupture: no tenderness or peritonism and stable findings. A tubal pregnancy reaching 12 weeks with a live fetus near the cornua suggests a proximal or interstitial tubal location.
Final diagnosis: Unruptured live left tubal (likely interstitial/proximal) ectopic pregnancy at 12 weeks' gestation

An asymptomatic primigravida at 12 weeks.
The gestational sac lies near the left uterine horn with an empty endometrial cavity.
MRI confirms a live 12-week fetus (CRL 5.8 cm) within the left fallopian tube.
There are no peritoneal signs, which indicates the pregnancy is unruptured.
Survival to 12 weeks near the cornu suggests implantation in the interstitial portion of the tube, which is surrounded by myometrium.
Unruptured left tubal ectopic pregnancy, interstitial portion
Ampullary or isthmic tubal ectopic pregnancy
Angular (eccentric intrauterine) pregnancy
Rudimentary horn pregnancy
Abdominal pregnancy
Interstitial tubal pregnancy.
For: located near the horn, empty cavity, MRI shows the sac in the tube, unruptured late survival.
Against: nothing significant.
Ampullary or isthmic pregnancy.
For: located in the tube.
Against: these usually rupture by 6 to 8 weeks, and this sac is next to the horn.
Angular pregnancy.
For: located near the horn.
Against: the endometrial cavity is empty and MRI places the sac in the tube.
Rudimentary horn pregnancy.
For: located near the horn and survived late.
Against: no Müllerian anomaly was identified.
Abdominal pregnancy.
Against: MRI shows the sac in the tube.
MRI excludes intrauterine, abdominal and horn pregnancies.
The cornual location and survival to 12 weeks favor the interstitial segment.
I commit to an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy.
Final diagnosis: Unruptured live left tubal (interstitial) ectopic pregnancy at 12 weeks' gestation.

Asymptomatic 30-year-old primigravida at 12 weeks of gestation with normal abdominal exam: Demonstrates an unruptured, clinically silent late first-trimester gestation.
Ultrasound showing gestation near the left uterine horn with an empty endometrial cavity: Strongly indicates an extrauterine (ectopic) pregnancy, specifically raising suspicion for an interstitial/cornual or proximal tubal location.
MRI confirming a live 12-week fetus (CRL 5.8 cm) located within the left fallopian tube: Definitively establishes an unruptured left tubal (interstitial/proximal) ectopic pregnancy.
Unruptured left tubal (interstitial) ectopic pregnancy
Rudimentary uterine horn pregnancy
Angular intrauterine pregnancy
Heterotopic pregnancy
Unruptured left tubal (interstitial) ectopic pregnancy:
For: Empty endometrial cavity on ultrasound; gestation situated near the left uterine horn; MRI directly confirms the live 12-week fetus is located within the left fallopian tube; absence of abdominal tenderness, guarding, or rigidity confirms it is unruptured.
Against: Survival of a tubal ectopic pregnancy to 12 weeks without rupture or pain is rare (most common in the interstitial segment, which has greater myometrial distensibility).
Rudimentary uterine horn pregnancy:
For: Can present as an asymptomatic 12-week live gestation near a uterine horn with an empty main endometrial cavity.
Against: MRI specifically localized the gestation to the left fallopian tube rather than a non-communicating rudimentary uterine horn.
Angular intrauterine pregnancy:
For: Gestation implanted near the uterotubal junction/uterine horn that can progress asymptomatically to 12 weeks.
Against: Angular pregnancy lies within the endometrial cavity medial to the uterotubal junction, whereas here the endometrial cavity is empty and MRI confirms a left fallopian tube location.
Heterotopic pregnancy:
For: Includes an ectopic pregnancy in the left fallopian tube.
Against: Ultrasound explicitly demonstrated an empty endometrial cavity, excluding a concurrent intrauterine gestation.
Heterotopic pregnancy is excluded by the empty endometrial cavity. Angular pregnancy and rudimentary uterine horn pregnancy are excluded by MRI confirmation that the gestational sac and live 12-week fetus reside within the left fallopian tube. The normal physical examination without peritoneal signs confirms it is unruptured. This commits the diagnosis to an unruptured left tubal (interstitial) ectopic pregnancy.
Final diagnosis: Unruptured left tubal (interstitial) ectopic pregnancy

A 13-year-old boy presents with a painless, clearly demarcated, spherical, bony-hard swelling on the buccal aspect of the right maxillary alveolar ridge, with intact overlying mucosa and vital adjacent teeth.
The absence of a family history of Gardner syndrome helps lower suspicion for syndromic multiple osteomas.
CBCT demonstrates an exophytic, mushroom-like radiodense lesion continuous with both the cortical and trabecular bone, which is characteristic of a bony exostosis.
Histopathology confirms bony trabeculae separated by connective tissue without a cartilaginous cap (ruling out osteochondroma), explicitly consistent with a benign exostosis/hyperostosis.
Given the anatomic site (buccal aspect of the maxillary alveolar ridge) and benign clinicopathologic features, the most likely diagnosis is a maxillary buccal exostosis.
Final diagnosis: Maxillary buccal exostosis

A 13-year-old has a painless, well-defined, bony-hard swelling on the buccal side of the right maxillary alveolar ridge. The overlying mucosa is intact and the adjacent teeth are vital, so an odontogenic or inflammatory cause is unlikely. CBCT shows an exophytic, mushroom-shaped radiodense mass that is continuous with the cortical and trabecular bone, which is typical of a reactive bony outgrowth. Histology shows bony trabeculae separated by connective tissue, consistent with benign exostosis/hyperostosis. There is no family history or other sign of Gardner syndrome, which argues against syndromic osteomas.
Final diagnosis: Buccal exostosis (benign bony exostosis) of the right maxillary alveolar ridge

A 13-year-old with a painless, well-demarcated, bony-hard swelling on the buccal right maxillary alveolar ridge (premolar–first molar). This points to a slow, benign bony process.
The overlying mucosa is intact, adjacent teeth are vital, and there is no trauma or parafunction history. This argues against odontogenic, inflammatory or reactive-traumatic causes.
CBCT shows an exophytic, mushroom-shaped radiodense mass continuous with both the cortical and trabecular bone. This is the hallmark of an exostosis or osteochondroma-type outgrowth rather than a separate tumour.
Histology shows bony trabeculae with intervening connective tissue, consistent with benign exostosis/hyperostosis.
There is no family history of Gardner syndrome, and the lesion is single. This makes a syndromic osteoma less likely.
Solitary buccal exostosis of the maxilla
Peripheral osteoma
Osteochondroma
Ossifying fibroma / fibrous dysplasia
Torus-like hyperostosis (atypical location)
Buccal exostosis.
For: buccal alveolar site, bony-hard, well-demarcated, continuity with cortex and medulla, benign trabecular histology.
Against: unusual at age 13 (more typical in adults) and no parafunction history.
Peripheral osteoma.
For: a radiodense, pedunculated/mushroom shape.
Against: osteomas are typically compact or cancellous bone tumours, and alveolar ridge involvement is less typical. Histology was reported as exostosis/hyperostosis, and there is no Gardner context.
Osteochondroma.
For: a mushroom-shaped lesion with cortico-medullary continuity.
Against: no cartilaginous cap was described on histology, and it is rare in the maxillary alveolus.
Ossifying fibroma / fibrous dysplasia.
For: young age and maxillary expansion.
Against: no ground-glass or mixed density, an exophytic rather than expansile intraosseous shape, and the histology is not fibro-osseous.
Torus.
For: a benign hyperostosis.
Against: tori occur at the palatal midline or lingual mandible, not the buccal maxillary ridge.
Fibro-osseous lesions are excluded on imaging and histology.
Torus is excluded by location.
Osteochondroma is excluded by the absence of cartilage.
Osteoma is less likely given the histology and location.
I commit to a benign buccal exostosis.
Final diagnosis: Solitary buccal exostosis (benign hyperostosis) of the right maxillary alveolar ridge.

Demographics and presentation: 13-year-old boy with a painless, slow-growing, spherical, bony-hard mass on the buccal aspect of the right maxillary alveolar ridge (first premolar to first molar) covered by intact, tense, pale mucosa; adjacent teeth have normal pulp vitality. Significance: Points toward a benign, non-odontogenic, surface osseous lesion.
Negative history: No trauma, parafunctional habits (bruxism/clenching), or family history of Gardner syndrome. Significance: Argues against reactive periostitis or syndromic multiple osteomas.
CBCT findings: Exophytic, mushroom-like, radiodense mass showing direct continuity with the underlying cortical and trabecular bone. Significance: Characteristic imaging hallmark of a benign exostosis or osteochondroma rather than an encapsulated or destructive neoplasm.
Histopathology: Bony trabeculae separated by connective tissue, consistent with benign exostosis/hyperostosis. Significance: Confirms a benign mature osseous proliferation and rules out malignancy or cartilaginous neoplasia.
Maxillary buccal exostosis (alveolar exostosis)
Peripheral (periosteal) osteoma
Osteochondroma
Ossifying fibroma (peripheral)
Maxillary buccal exostosis:
For: Classic location on the buccal aspect of the maxillary alveolar ridge; painless, bony-hard, well-demarcated enlargement with intact overlying mucosa; vital adjacent teeth; CBCT showing exophytic radiodense growth continuous with cortical and trabecular bone; histopathology confirming benign exostosis/hyperostosis.
Against: Typically presents in adults and is often bilateral/multiple, whereas this patient is 13 years old with a solitary lesion; no reported bruxism or occlusal trauma.
Peripheral osteoma:
For: Painless, solitary, bony-hard, well-circumscribed exophytic radiodense mass on the maxilla; histologically composed of mature bone.
Against: Less commonly arises on the buccal alveolar ridge compared to the mandibular angle or paranasal sinuses; no family history of Gardner syndrome; histopathology specifically favors benign exostosis/hyperostosis.
Osteochondroma:
For: Mushroom-like exophytic bony lesion with continuity to both cortical and trabecular bone on CBCT; occurs in adolescents.
Against: Extremely rare in the maxillary alveolar ridge (typically affects the mandibular condyle or coronoid process); histopathology shows only bony trabeculae and connective tissue without the diagnostic hyaline cartilage cap.
Peripheral ossifying fibroma:
For: Occurs on the maxillary gingiva/alveolar ridge in adolescents and young adults.
Against: Typically presents as a soft-to-firm gingival mass rather than a bony-hard mass continuous with cortical/trabecular bone on CBCT; histopathology lacks cellular fibrous stroma with variable calcifications.
Osteochondroma is excluded due to the absence of a cartilaginous cap on histopathology.
Peripheral ossifying fibroma is excluded by the bony-hard consistency, direct continuity with cortical and trabecular bone on CBCT, and mature osseous histopathology.
Peripheral osteoma is less favored given the classic buccal alveolar ridge location, absence of Gardner syndrome, and histopathological confirmation of benign exostosis/hyperostosis.
Commitment: The combination of classic buccal maxillary alveolar location, CBCT continuity with cortical/trabecular bone, vital adjacent teeth, and confirmatory histopathology establishes maxillary buccal exostosis.
Final diagnosis: Maxillary buccal exostosis

History of uterine trauma: 34-year-old woman presenting 2 months after dilation and curettage (D&C) for a 15-week missed abortion. Significance: Uterine instrumentation is the primary risk factor for acquired uterine vascular anomalies.
Severe hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability: Menorrhagia with clots, severe cramping, fatigue, confusion, and presyncope. Significance: Classic presentation of high-flow arterial uterine bleeding rather than routine post-abortal spotting.
TVUS and MRI findings: Echogenic mass with markedly increased blood flow on TVUS; mixed endometrial mass with serpiginous vessel flow voids and solid enhancement on MRI. Significance: Narrows the differential to hypervascular retained products of conception (RPOC), gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD), or a vascular malformation.
CTA and selective angiography: Cluster of vessels with early venous filling on CTA, supplied by the left uterine artery on selective angiography. Significance: Early venous filling (arteriovenous shunting) is pathognomonic for an arteriovenous malformation.
Acquired uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM)
Retained products of conception (RPOC) with enhanced myometrial vascularity
Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN)
Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm
Acquired uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM):
For: Recent D&C (uterine trauma); delayed, torrential abnormal uterine bleeding causing hemodynamic instability; serpiginous vessels on MRI; CTA showing a cluster of vessels with early venous filling; selective angiography confirming arterial supply from the left uterine artery.
Against: Initial ultrasound and MRI showed an echogenic/solid endometrial mass component, which can mimic RPOC.
Retained products of conception (RPOC):
For: Recent missed abortion and D&C; echogenic endometrial mass with increased vascularity on TVUS and solid enhancement on MRI.
Against: Does not explain the classic vascular nidus with early venous filling (AV shunting) confirmed on CTA and angiography.
Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN):
For: Post-pregnancy abnormal bleeding and hypervascular uterine mass on TVUS/MRI.
Against: Prior pregnancy was a documented missed abortion rather than a molar pregnancy, no hCG elevation is reported, and CTA/angiography specifically confirms a vascular cluster with early venous filling rather than a malignant trophoblastic tumor.
Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm:
For: Occurs after D&C and causes severe delayed hemorrhage.
Against: Typically appears as a single saccular outpouching with turbulent ("yin-yang") flow rather than a cluster of serpiginous vessels with early venous filling.
Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm is excluded by the presence of a vessel cluster and early venous filling rather than a focal saccular arterial dilatation.
GTN is excluded by the lack of supporting clinical/biochemical features and definitive angiographic demonstration of an arteriovenous shunt.
RPOC (though initially suspected and sometimes coexistent) cannot account for the definitive arteriovenous shunting seen on CTA and selective angiography.
Commitment: Post-D&C torrential hemorrhage combined with serpiginous vessels on MRI and early venous filling supplied by the left uterine artery on CTA/angiography is diagnostic of an acquired uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM).
Final diagnosis: Acquired uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM)

The patient had uterine trauma from a D&C for missed abortion and then developed heavy, irregular bleeding with clots and hemodynamic instability. Ultrasound shows an echogenic mass with increased blood flow, so the main question is retained products of conception versus a vascular lesion. MRI shows serpiginous flow voids. CTA shows a cluster of vessels with early venous filling, which means arteriovenous shunting. Selective angiography identifies feeders from the left uterine artery. Together these fit an acquired arteriovenous malformation after instrumentation.
Final diagnosis: Acquired uterine arteriovenous malformation (post-D&C)

A 34-year-old woman presents with severe abnormal uterine bleeding, menorrhagia with clots, and signs of hemodynamic instability 2 months after a D&C for a missed abortion. Uterine instrumentation (D&C) is a major risk factor for acquired uterine vascular malformations.
Initial TVUS and MRI show an echogenic/mixed endometrial mass with increased vascularity and serpiginous vessel signals, narrowing the differential to retained products of conception (RPOC) versus a uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM).
CTA demonstrates a cluster of vessels with early venous filling, which is the hallmark diagnostic feature of an arteriovenous shunt/malformation rather than simple RPOC.
Selective angiography confirms the diagnosis by identifying the left uterine artery as the feeding vessel supplying the vascular malformation.
Final diagnosis: Acquired uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM)

Prior D&C (uterine instrumentation) after a 15-week missed abortion. This is a classic risk factor for acquired vascular lesions.
Two months later: heavy bleeding with clots, presyncope, confusion and hemodynamic instability. This indicates a high-flow bleeding source.

Selective angiography identifies a feeding left uterine artery.
Acquired uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM)
Retained products of conception (RPOC) with enhanced myometrial vascularity
Gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD)
Uterine artery pseudoaneurysm
Placental polyp

For: post-D&C timing, a hypervascular mass, serpiginous vessels, early venous filling on CTA, and a uterine artery feeder on angiography.
Against: overlapping ultrasound appearance with RPOC.
RPOC with enhanced vascularity.
For: an echogenic endometrial mass, the earlier ultrasound suggesting RPOC, and a recent pregnancy.
Against: RPOC does not cause arteriovenous shunting with early venous filling.
GTD.
For: post-pregnancy bleeding and a vascular mass.
Against: no β-hCG elevation or invasive mass was described, and the angiographic picture is of shunting rather than a tumour.
Pseudoaneurysm.
For: post-instrumentation timing and the bleeding pattern.
Against: imaging shows a vessel cluster rather than a single saccular outpouching.

Against: no AV shunting.

GTD and pseudoaneurysm do not fit the morphology.
I commit to an acquired AVM. Coexisting retained tissue is possible but is not the primary bleeding source.
Final diagnosis: Acquired uterine arteriovenous malformation (post-D&C), supplied by the left uterine artery.

A 66-year-old woman presents with subacute, rapidly progressive cognitive decline, weakness, falls, aphasia, hallucinations, and SIADH, proving fatal within four months despite unremarkable infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, and paraneoplastic workups.
CSF analysis shows pleocytosis and elevated IL-10, a highly specific biomarker for primary CNS B-cell lymphoma.
Initial MRI reveals diffuse, non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintensities without mass effect or restricted diffusion, which is the classic radiological signature of lymphomatosis cerebri—a rare, diffusely infiltrating variant of primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL).
MR spectroscopy confirms a hypercellular neoplastic process (elevated choline:creatine ratio, decreased NAA), and follow-up MRI shows new diffusion restriction and hyperperfusion in the caudate and hippocampus (consistent with superimposed focal lymphoma progression or ischemia).
Autopsy confirmation of CD20-positive B cells establishes the diagnosis of lymphomatosis cerebri (primary CNS diffuse large B-cell lymphoma).
Final diagnosis: Lymphomatosis cerebri (diffuse variant of primary central nervous system diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)

Rapidly progressive neurological decline: 66-year-old woman with subacute cognitive decline, confusion, hallucinations, expressive aphasia, progressive weakness, intermittent fevers, and SIADH leading to death within 4 months despite treatment. Significance: Indicates an aggressive, diffuse CNS infiltrative or neoplastic process.
CSF biomarker: CSF pleocytosis with elevated IL-10, alongside negative infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, and paraneoplastic panels. Significance: Elevated CSF IL-10 is a highly specific biomarker for primary CNS B-cell lymphoma.
Characteristic neuroimaging evolution: Initial MRI showed diffuse, non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintensities without mass effect or restricted diffusion; follow-up MRI showed new asymmetric diffusion restriction and hyperperfusion in the caudate and hippocampus; MR spectroscopy showed elevated Cho:Cr and decreased NAA. Significance: Diffuse non-enhancing leukoencephalopathy with neoplastic spectroscopy (high Cho:Cr, low NAA) is the hallmark of lymphomatosis cerebri, while subsequent focal diffusion restriction indicates superimposed ischemic infarction or focal high-grade lymphomatous infiltration.
Autopsy confirmation: Infiltration by CD20-positive B cells with superimposed focal lesions in the caudate and hippocampus. Significance: Pathologically confirms a diffuse B-cell CNS lymphoma (lymphomatosis cerebri).
Lymphomatosis cerebri (diffuse variant of primary CNS diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVLBCL)
Gliomatosis cerebri (diffuse infiltrating glioma)
Autoimmune or infectious encephalitis (e.g., viral, prion disease / CJD)
Lymphomatosis cerebri (primary CNS diffuse large B-cell lymphoma):
For: Subacute rapidly progressive dementia, aphasia, weakness, and fatal course; elevated CSF IL-10 and pleocytosis; classic initial MRI of diffuse, non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintensities without mass effect; hypercellular/neoplastic MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho:Cr, decreased NAA); autopsy confirming CD20-positive B-cell infiltration (with superimposed focal infarcts/lymphomatous transformation in the caudate and hippocampus).
Against: None; accounts for the entire clinical, biochemical, radiologic, and autopsy profile.
Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (IVLBCL):
For: CD20-positive B cells, subacute encephalopathy, intermittent fevers, SIADH, and multifocal diffusion restriction (infarcts) on follow-up MRI.
Against: Typically presents early with multifocal acute/subacute infarcts and patchy enhancement rather than initial diffuse, non-enhancing T2/FLAIR white matter hyperintensities without restricted diffusion; however, it remains the closest B-cell mimic.
Gliomatosis cerebri:
For: Diffuse, non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintensities without discrete mass effect and elevated Cho:Cr with decreased NAA on MR spectroscopy.
Against: Excluded by elevated CSF IL-10 and autopsy demonstrating CD20-positive B cells rather than glial tumor cells.
Autoimmune or infectious encephalitis / CJD:
For: Rapidly progressive dementia, hallucinations, aphasia, CSF pleocytosis, and asymmetric caudate/hippocampal diffusion restriction.
Against: Broad infectious, autoimmune, and paraneoplastic workups were negative; MR spectroscopy indicated a hypercellular neoplasm; autopsy confirmed CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma.
Autoimmune/infectious encephalitis and prion disease are excluded by negative panels, neoplastic MR spectroscopy, elevated CSF IL-10, and CD20+ B-cell pathology.
Gliomatosis cerebri is excluded by elevated CSF IL-10 and CD20+ B-cell autopsy confirmation.
IVLBCL is less favored than lymphomatosis cerebri given the initial diffuse, non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintensities without restricted diffusion or mass effect.
Commitment: The combination of subacute fatal cognitive decline, elevated CSF IL-10, initial diffuse non-enhancing T2/FLAIR hyperintensities with hypercellular MR spectroscopy, and autopsy-proven CD20-positive B-cell infiltration establishes lymphomatosis cerebri (primary CNS diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) with superimposed focal ischemia/infarction (or focal lymphomatous lesions) in the caudate and hippocampus.
Final diagnosis: Lymphomatosis cerebri (diffuse primary CNS B-cell lymphoma) with superimposed focal infarction/involvement of the caudate nucleus and hippocampus

A long-standing, soft, mobile, painless mass, which suggests a benign process. Imaging shows a large, circumscribed, fat-containing mass with mixed density ("breast within a breast"), the classic hamartoma appearance. An internal spiculated component with microcalcifications and plateau kinetics was graded BI-RADS 5 and mimicked carcinoma. Core biopsy and excision both showed disorganized ducts, lobules, fibrous tissue and fat without atypia or mitoses.
(1) Breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma); (2) invasive carcinoma arising in or near a hamartoma; (3) lipoma or liposarcoma; (4) phyllodes tumor; (5) fat necrosis.
Hamartoma. For: encapsulated fatty-glandular imaging, years of stability, and diagnostic histology. Against: the spiculated BI-RADS 5 focus, explained here by internal fibroglandular change.
Carcinoma in a hamartoma. For: spiculation, microcalcifications, plateau kinetics. Against: no atypia or malignancy on either core or excision.
Lipoma or liposarcoma. For: the fatty component. Against: the glandular elements, and no lipoblasts or atypia.
Phyllodes tumor. For: a large circumscribed mass. Against: no leaf-like stromal hypercellularity and no mitoses.
Fat necrosis. For: spiculation and calcification in fat. Against: no trauma history; histology shows organized benign mixed tissue rather than necrosis.
The excision histology excludes malignancy, phyllodes tumor and lipomatous tumors. I commit to a hamartoma whose internal component mimicked malignancy.
Final diagnosis: Breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma) with a malignancy-mimicking internal spiculated component

Core biopsy and the excised specimen showed a well-circumscribed lesion with disorganized ducts, lobules, fibrous stroma and fat, with no atypia or mitoses. These features are diagnostic of a mammary hamartoma.

A 46-year-old woman presents with a longstanding, painless, soft, mobile mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast.
Although mammography and MRI raised high suspicion for malignancy (BI-RADS V) due to an internal spiculated, enhancing area with microcalcifications, the overall lesion was a large (9.5 × 7.5 × 8 cm), circumscribed, predominantly fatty mass.
Core needle biopsy and final surgical excision pathology confirmed a well-circumscribed benign lesion composed of disorganized glandular (ducts and lobules), fibrous, and adipose tissues without atypia or mitotic activity, which is the defining histological appearance of a breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma).
Final diagnosis: Breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma)

46-year-old woman with a long-standing, painless, soft, mobile palpable mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast: Clinical features strongly favor a benign, slow-growing breast lesion.
Mammography and MRI showing a large (9.5 × 7.5 × 8 cm) predominantly fatty, circumscribed mass containing a 4.5 × 4 × 3 cm irregular, spiculated, enhancing internal lesion with microcalcifications (BI-RADS V): The predominantly fatty, well-circumscribed outer mass is classic for a hamartoma, while the internal spiculated, enhancing component mimics invasive breast carcinoma.
Core needle biopsy and complete surgical excision demonstrating a well-circumscribed benign tumor composed of disorganized glandular (ducts and lobules), fibrous, and adipose tissue without cytoarchitectural atypia or mitosis: Pathognomonic histopathology of a breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma) and definitively rules out malignancy despite BI-RADS V imaging.
Breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma)
Invasive ductal carcinoma (arising within a hamartoma or de novo)
Breast lipoma
Giant fibroadenoma
Phyllodes tumor
Breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma): For: Long-standing, painless, soft, mobile mass; mammography and MRI show a large predominantly fatty, well-circumscribed oval mass; both core biopsy and surgical excision pathology show a well-circumscribed benign tumor with disorganized normal breast elements (ducts, lobules, fibrous stroma, and adipose tissue) without atypia or mitosis. Against: Internal spiculated, heterogeneously enhancing lesion with microcalcifications (BI-RADS V) mimicked malignancy on imaging, though internal fibrosis/adenosis within a hamartoma can produce this appearance.
Invasive ductal carcinoma (de novo or within a hamartoma): For: Internal 4.5 × 4 × 3 cm lesion with spiculated borders, microcalcifications, and heterogeneous enhancement with plateau kinetics assigned BI-RADS V on both mammography and MRI. Against: Definitively excluded by both core needle biopsy and complete surgical excision pathology showing entirely benign disorganized tissue with no cytoarchitectural atypia or mitotic activity.
Breast lipoma: For: Painless, soft, mobile, circumscribed, predominantly fatty breast mass present for years. Against: Contains substantial dense internal glandular and fibrous elements on imaging and pathology, whereas a lipoma consists purely of mature adipocytes.
Giant fibroadenoma: For: Large, painless, mobile, well-circumscribed benign breast mass. Against: Predominantly fatty composition on imaging and disorganized admixture of lobules, ducts, fibrous tissue, and abundant adipose tissue on histology are characteristic of hamartoma rather than fibroadenoma.
Phyllodes tumor: For: Large, well-circumscribed breast mass in a 46-year-old woman. Against: Lacks stromal hypercellularity, leaf-like architecture, atypia, or mitotic activity on surgical excision, and has a predominantly fatty radiographic appearance.
Invasive carcinoma (including carcinoma arising within a hamartoma) is definitively excluded by complete surgical excision pathology confirming the absence of atypia or mitoses. Lipoma is excluded by the presence of glandular and fibrous components, and fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor are excluded by the predominantly fatty architecture and disorganized normal mammary tissue without stromal proliferation. I commit to breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma).
Final diagnosis: Breast hamartoma (fibroadenolipoma)

Bacteremia with concordant GI pathogen on FilmArray: Both blood cultures and stool FilmArray GI panel are positive for the same bacterial pathogen in a 71-year-old man with fever (38.5 °C), confusion, marked neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 23,900/mm³, 92.1% neutrophils), and elevated CRP (12.6 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (2.04 ng/mL).
Delayed bacteremia following self-limiting diarrhea: A 5-day self-limiting diarrheal illness 2 months earlier with persistent fecal carriage leading to invasive bloodstream infection in an elderly host with advanced metastatic lung cancer.
Negative pleural fluid culture: Rules out empyema or procedural contamination from the pleural drainage 10 days prior.
Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) bacteremia
Campylobacter (C. jejuni / C. coli) bacteremia
Yersinia enterocolitica bacteremia
Plesiomonas shigelloides or Vibrio bacteremia
Procedure-related empyema / nosocomial bacteremia (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas)
Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) bacteremia:
For: Classic pathogen detected on the FilmArray GI panel; uniquely known for causing self-limiting gastroenteritis followed by prolonged asymptomatic stool carriage (weeks to months) and subsequent secondary bacteremia/sepsis in elderly or immunocompromised cancer patients; no travel history required.
Against: None; every clinical, temporal, and microbiologic feature aligns tightly.
Campylobacter (C. jejuni / C. coli) bacteremia:
For: Included on the FilmArray GI panel and can cause bacteremia in immunocompromised hosts.
Against: Bacteremia typically occurs acutely during the diarrheal illness rather than 2 months after a self-limiting episode; C. fetus (the species most prone to bacteremia without acute diarrhea) is not detected by the standard FilmArray GI panel.
Yersinia enterocolitica bacteremia:
For: Included on the FilmArray GI panel and can cause bacteremia in compromised hosts.
Against: Strongly associated with iron overload, hemochromatosis, or cirrhosis rather than advanced lung cancer; prolonged 2-month carrier state leading to delayed sepsis is much less typical than with Salmonella.
Plesiomonas shigelloides or Vibrio bacteremia:
For: Included on the FilmArray GI panel.
Against: Typically associated with seafood/brackish water exposure, travel, or chronic liver disease, and rarely cause delayed bacteremia 2 months after self-limiting diarrhea.
Procedure-related empyema / nosocomial bacteremia:
For: Recent pleural drainage 10 days prior.
Against: Pleural drainage culture was negative, and the bloodstream organism was simultaneously identified on the stool FilmArray GI panel.
Excluded: Procedure-related empyema is excluded by negative pleural fluid cultures and the matching stool FilmArray pathogen. Vibrio and Plesiomonas are unlikely without relevant exposure or cirrhosis. Campylobacter and Yersinia are less consistent with delayed bacteremia 2 months after self-limiting diarrhea in an oncology patient without iron overload.
Commitment: The combination of advanced malignancy, self-limiting diarrhea 2 months prior, acute sepsis with marked neutrophilic leukocytosis, and concordant positivity on blood culture and FilmArray GI panel commits to non-typhoidal Salmonella bacteremia.
Final diagnosis: Non-typhoidal Salmonella bacteremia

Localized (unicentric) Castleman disease
Sclerosing mesenteritis
Desmoid fibromatosis
For: infiltration into adjacent fat and organs, large size, no metastases, benign on frozen section.
Against: necrosis is unusual, though large tumors can degenerate; recurrence is common, so one year is a short follow-up.
Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor
For: infiltrative mass in a middle-aged adult, benign appearance.
Against: no fever, anemia or inflammatory syndrome.
GIST
For: large necrotic mass next to the stomach.
Against: intraoperative pathology non-malignant; it is extraluminal and infiltrative rather than arising from the bowel wall.
Castleman disease
For: well-vascularized and benign.
Against: usually well circumscribed, not infiltrative, and rarely necrotic.
Sclerosing mesenteritis
For: infiltrates mesenteric fat.
Against: rarely forms a large necrotic mass needing gastrectomy.

Castleman disease and sclerosing mesenteritis do not match the morphology.
IMT lacks inflammatory features.
Commitment: desmoid-type fibromatosis, accepting that definitive histology could favor IMT.
Final diagnosis: Intra-abdominal (mesenteric) desmoid-type fibromatosis.

This 55-year-old female presented with progressive epigastric/periumbilical pain, nausea, and anorexia. Imaging revealed a large, necrotic peritoneal mass infiltrating adjacent fat and adhering to the stomach, pancreas, and transverse colon—features that strongly mimic a locally aggressive intra-abdominal malignancy—yet without distant metastasis. Surgical resection (partial gastrectomy and segmental colectomy) and pathology demonstrated a nonmalignant, well-vascularized mass with no recurrence at 1 year. A benign, locally adherent, well-vascularized peritoneal mass with necrosis that mimics malignancy and is cured by complete resection is most characteristic of an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.
Final diagnosis: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT)

Locally aggressive peritoneal mass mimicking malignancy: Large necrotic, well-vascularized perigastric/peritoneal mass infiltrating adjacent fat and densely adhering to the stomach, pancreas, and transverse colon, requiring en bloc partial gastrectomy and segmental colectomy.
Nonmalignant pathology with no metastasis or recurrence: Intraoperative and definitive pathology confirmed a nonmalignant lesion, with no evidence of metastasis on CT and no recurrence at 1-year clinical and radiologic follow-up.
Subacute nonspecific symptoms in a healthy 55-year-old woman: 2 weeks of worsening diffuse abdominal pain, nausea, and anorexia without fever, weight loss, or prior surgical history.
Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) / inflammatory pseudotumor
Mesenteric fibromatosis (desmoid tumor)
Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) of the peritoneum/mesentery
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST)
Unicentric Castleman disease
Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) / inflammatory pseudotumor:
For: Classic nonmalignant/intermediate mesenchymal lesion that closely mimics intra-abdominal malignancy on CT; frequently well-vascularized with central necrosis, infiltrates adjacent fat, and densely adheres to stomach, pancreas, and transverse colon requiring multivisceral resection; low recurrence after complete surgical excision.
Against: More frequently seen in children and young adults, though well documented in middle-aged adults.
Mesenteric fibromatosis (desmoid tumor):
For: Nonmalignant, locally infiltrative peritoneal/mesenteric mass adhering to bowel and adjacent organs.
Against: Typically homogenous, hypovascular, and non-necrotic on CT/intraoperative exam (unlike this well-vascularized, necrotic mass), and carries a high local recurrence rate.
Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) of the peritoneum/mesentery:
For: Can present as a large, well-vascularized, nonmalignant peritoneal mass with areas of necrosis.
Against: Typically well-circumscribed and encapsulated rather than diffusely infiltrating adjacent fat and adhering densely to three separate organs (stomach, pancreas, transverse colon).
Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST):
For: Classic large, hypervascular, necrotic perigastric mass adhering to adjacent organs in a 55-year-old.
Against: Excluded because intraoperative and definitive pathology confirmed a nonmalignant mass.
Unicentric Castleman disease:
For: Benign, hypervascular peritoneal/retroperitoneal mass cured by resection.
Against: Typically well-circumscribed without necrosis or extensive infiltration of adjacent fat and adherence to stomach, pancreas, and colon.
Excluded: GIST (and other sarcomas/carcinomas) is excluded by nonmalignant histopathology. Desmoid tumor is less consistent with a well-vascularized, necrotic mass without recurrence. SFT and Castleman disease are typically well-circumscribed rather than infiltrating surrounding fat and densely adhering to stomach, pancreas, and colon.
Commitment: A nonmalignant, well-vascularized, necrotic peritoneal mass infiltrating fat and densely adhering to adjacent organs requiring multivisceral resection, with no metastasis or recurrence at 1 year, commits to inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT).
Final diagnosis: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT)

A middle-aged woman has a large, partly necrotic intraperitoneal mass in the perigastric region. It infiltrates adjacent fat and adheres to the stomach, pancreas and transverse colon, with no metastases. Intraoperative pathology called it nonmalignant, but it was locally aggressive enough to need en bloc colectomy and partial gastrectomy. A benign but locally infiltrative intra-abdominal mesenchymal tumor that does not metastasize best fits desmoid-type fibromatosis. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor is the main alternative. There was no recurrence at one year.
Final diagnosis: Intra-abdominal (mesenteric/omental) desmoid-type fibromatosis (aggressive fibromatosis)

Severe neuropathic pain (stabbing, shock-like, burning) starting about 21 days after dengue. This latency points to a post-infectious, immune-mediated process.
Proximal-predominant amyotrophy and paresis of the right arm (deltoid, infraspinatus, biceps). This matches upper and middle trunk (C5–C7) territory.
The right upper limb shows allodynia, thermal hyperesthesia, deep hypoesthesia, absent reflexes and hypotonia. This is a lower motor neuron and sensory pattern confined to one limb.
ENMG shows acute denervation with increased latency, which means peripheral nerve or plexus injury.
MRI shows signal change in the upper and middle trunks of the brachial plexus. This localizes the lesion to the plexus.
Dengue IgM is positive and other inflammatory, infectious and immune work-up is normal, which supports dengue as the trigger.
Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome) triggered by dengue
Guillain-Barré syndrome after dengue
Cervical radiculopathy (C5–C6)
Complex regional pain syndrome
Dengue-associated myositis
Parsonage-Turner syndrome:
For: severe pain followed by weakness and atrophy, post-viral latency, one limb, proximal muscles, plexus changes on MRI, denervation on ENMG.
Against: nothing significant.
Guillain-Barré syndrome:
For: post-infectious timing, areflexia.
Against: only one limb is affected, there is no ascending or symmetric weakness, and severe focal pain is atypical.
Cervical radiculopathy:
For: C5–C6 distribution.
Against: lesion is in the plexus trunks on MRI, onset was acute after infection, and no spinal cause is described.
CRPS:
For: allodynia, livedo, burning pain.
Against: objective denervation, areflexia and plexus lesion show true nerve injury.
Myositis:
For: post-viral weakness.
Against: neuropathic pain, sensory loss, areflexia and an ENMG pattern of denervation rather than myopathy.
GBS is excluded because the deficit is unilateral and focal.
Radiculopathy is excluded because MRI localizes to the plexus.
CRPS and myositis are excluded because of the objective neurogenic findings.
I commit to dengue-triggered neuralgic amyotrophy.
Final diagnosis: Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy / acute brachial plexus neuritis) of the right upper and middle trunks after dengue infection.

Severe acute neuropathic pain (stabbing, shock-like, burning) in the proximal and intermediate right arm developing approximately 21 days after dengue virus infection, confirmed by positive dengue IgM serology — classic post-infectious immune-mediated latency.
Rapidly ensuing proximal upper-limb amyotrophy, hypotonia, grade 2/3 paresis of the deltoid, infraspinatus, and biceps brachii (C5–C6 / upper brachial plexus distribution), deep hypoesthesia, areflexia, and sensory hypersensitivity (allodynia, thermal hyperesthesia) — localizes to a patchy, predominantly motor-and-sensory brachial plexopathy.

Brachial plexus MRI showing subtle signal changes in the upper and middle primary trunks with normal cranial nerves and unremarkable workup for other inflammatory, infectious, or autoimmune causes — directly confirms brachial plexus involvement.

Dengue-associated Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy):
For: Classic biphasic pattern of severe acute proximal shoulder/arm neuropathic pain followed by patchy weakness and rapid amyotrophy in upper/middle trunk muscles (deltoid, infraspinatus, biceps); clear post-infectious trigger (~21 days post-dengue with positive IgM); acute denervation on ENMG; MRI signal abnormality localized to the upper and middle primary trunks; normal workup for other etiologies.
Against: Livedo and marked allodynia/thermal hyperesthesia are less typical than pure motor-predominant presentations, though autonomic and sensory fiber involvement can occur.
Cervical radiculopathy (C5–C6):
For: Pain, weakness in deltoid/infraspinatus/biceps, sensory loss, and reduced/absent reflexes in a C5–C6 distribution.
Against: MRI demonstrates signal changes in the brachial plexus trunks rather than cervical root compression; severe burning/shock-like pain with rapid amyotrophy and livedo 3 weeks post-dengue strongly favors immune-mediated plexitis over structural radiculopathy.
Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS):
For: Severe burning pain, allodynia, thermal hyperesthesia, and skin discoloration (livedo) with functional impairment.
Against: CRPS does not explain acute axonal denervation on ENMG, MRI signal changes in the upper and middle brachial plexus trunks, or selective proximal myotomal paresis and amyotrophy; there is also no preceding limb trauma.
Guillain-Barré syndrome (focal/brachial variant):
For: Post-infectious onset (~3 weeks after dengue virus infection), acute weakness, hypotonia, and areflexia.
Against: Strictly unilateral focal involvement of one brachial plexus with severe localized neuropathic pain, rapid amyotrophy, normal cranial nerves, and MRI signal changes confined to the right upper/middle trunks argue strongly against GBS, which is typically symmetric and polyradiculoneuropathic.
Neoplastic or compressive brachial plexopathy:
For: Unilateral brachial plexus pain, weakness, sensory deficits, and denervation on ENMG.
Against: No mass lesion on brachial plexus MRI, acute post-dengue onset, and preferential involvement of the upper/middle trunks (neoplastic plexopathy more often affects the lower trunk, as in Pancoast tumors).
Cervical radiculopathy and compressive/neoplastic plexopathy are excluded by the absence of a compressive or mass lesion and the direct localization of signal changes to the upper and middle primary trunks on MRI. CRPS is excluded because it cannot account for objective acute denervation on ENMG and brachial plexus MRI abnormalities. GBS is excluded by the strictly unilateral, painful, trunk-localized plexopathy with normal cranial nerves. By direct temporal association with confirmed dengue infection, classic severe neuropathic pain followed by proximal amyotrophy, ENMG evidence of acute denervation, and MRI confirmation of upper and middle trunk involvement, the diagnosis commits to dengue-associated Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy).
Final diagnosis: Dengue-associated Parsonage-Turner syndrome (post-infectious neuralgic amyotrophy / brachial plexitis)

A 63-year-old female developed acute, severe neuropathic pain (stabbing, shock-like, burning) in the proximal right arm approximately 3 weeks after a confirmed dengue virus infection (positive IgM).
The severe pain was followed by rapid-onset amyotrophy, hypotonia, paresis of proximal shoulder/arm muscles (deltoid, infraspinatus, biceps brachii), sensory abnormalities (allodynia, thermal hyperesthesia, deep hypoesthesia), and absent tendon reflexes in the affected limb.
Electroneuromyography confirms acute peripheral nerve denervation, and brachial plexus MRI demonstrates subtle signal changes in the upper and middle primary trunks, localizing the pathology to the brachial plexus while excluding other inflammatory, infectious, or immune-mediated etiologies.
The classic triad of a preceding viral trigger (dengue), acute severe shoulder/arm neuropathic pain, and subsequent patchy proximal upper limb weakness and amyotrophy is diagnostic of post-infectious neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome).
Final diagnosis: Post-dengue Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy / brachial plexitis)

A 63-year-old woman develops severe neuropathic pain in the proximal right arm about 3 weeks after a dengue infection. The pain is followed by amyotrophy, weakness in the deltoid, infraspinatus and biceps (upper and middle trunk distribution), sensory changes, absent reflexes and autonomic signs (livedo). ENMG shows acute denervation, and MRI shows signal change in the upper and middle trunks of the brachial plexus. Other inflammatory, infectious and immune causes were excluded. This sequence of acute severe pain, then patchy weakness and atrophy of the shoulder girdle and arm after a viral trigger, is classic neuralgic amyotrophy.
Final diagnosis: Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy / acute brachial plexus neuritis) following dengue virus infection

Pathognomonic skin signs: Gottron's papules and a shawl sign, with a photodistributed rash. The rash appears hyperpigmented rather than violaceous, which is common in darker skin.
Symmetric proximal weakness (3/5) with oropharyngeal dysphagia.
Raised aldolase, LDH and AST with normal CK. A normal CK is typical of anti-MDA5 disease.
EMG, MRI edema and biopsy all show inflammatory myopathy. The biopsy shows perifascicular pathology, the hallmark of dermatomyositis.
Anti-MDA5 and anti-SAE1 positive. These are dermatomyositis-specific antibodies. MDA5 carries a risk of rapidly progressive ILD; SAE1 is associated with dysphagia and, in adults, malignancy.
CT chest with no ILD at present.
Hyporeflexia. This is explained by weakness, since EMG shows no neuropathy.
Dermatomyositis (anti-MDA5 and anti-SAE1 positive) with myositis and dysphagia, without ILD

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy

Dermatomyositis. For: Gottron's papules, shawl sign, perifascicular atrophy and specific antibodies. Against: normal CK, which is explained by the MDA5 phenotype.
SLE or overlap. For: young Hispanic woman, ANA 1:320 and photosensitive rash. Against: no anti-dsDNA, cytopenias or renal disease; Gottron's papules and perifascicular pathology point to dermatomyositis.
Polymyositis or antisynthetase syndrome. Against: skin findings, no anti-synthetase antibody and no ILD.
Necrotizing myopathy. Against: normal CK and perifascicular inflammatory pathology rather than necrosis.
Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis. For: SAE1 positivity. Against: age 19, with no tumor identified (age-appropriate screening is still reasonable).
I exclude the alternatives on the skin findings, biopsy and serology. I commit to dermatomyositis, while noting the need to monitor for ILD because of MDA5 positivity.
Final diagnosis: Dermatomyositis, positive for anti-MDA5 and anti-SAE1, with proximal and oropharyngeal myopathy and no current interstitial lung disease.

Laboratory testing shows elevated inflammatory markers, elevated AST, ALT, LDH, and aldolase (despite normal CK and myoglobin), positive ANA, and a myositis antibody panel positive for both anti-SAE1 and anti-MDA5 autoantibodies. 4-month progressive symmetrical proximal muscle weakness (3/5) and oropharyngeal dysphagia (confirmed on modified barium swallow): Classic clinical presentation of an inflammatory myopathy involving skeletal and bulbar musculature.
Pathognomonic cutaneous findings (Gottron’s papules on bilateral dorsal joints and hyperpigmented rash in a shawl sign distribution on sun-exposed areas): Clinically diagnostic of dermatomyositis.
Elevated muscle-associated enzymes (AST, ALT, LDH, aldolase) with normal CK and myoglobin: Recognizable pattern in certain dermatomyositis subsets (notably anti-MDA5 and anti-SAE1) where CK can be normal despite active myositis, while aldolase and transaminases are elevated.
EMG (acute inflammatory myopathy), MRI (diffuse muscle edema/enhancement), and muscle biopsy (severe inflammatory myopathy with perifascicular pathology): Perifascicular pathology on biopsy is the histological hallmark of dermatomyositis.
Positive myositis-specific antibodies (anti-SAE1 and anti-MDA5) and ANA (1:320 nuclear speckled): Serologically confirms dermatomyositis; anti-SAE1 is classically associated with severe skin disease and dysphagia.
Normal chest CT: Rules out concomitant interstitial lung disease (ILD) at presentation, which is critical to screen for given anti-MDA5 positivity.
Dermatomyositis (anti-SAE1 and anti-MDA5 positive)
Polymyositis / immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with secondary myositis
Inclusion body myositis (IBM)
Myasthenia gravis
Dermatomyositis (anti-SAE1 and anti-MDA5 positive):
For: Symmetrical proximal weakness, dysphagia, pathognomonic Gottron’s papules and shawl sign, elevated aldolase/LDH/AST/ALT, EMG and MRI showing inflammatory myopathy, muscle biopsy showing perifascicular pathology, and positive myositis-specific antibodies (anti-SAE1 and anti-MDA5).
Against: Normal CK and myoglobin (a known pitfall in dermatomyositis, especially anti-MDA5/anti-SAE1 subsets, and outweighed by elevated aldolase, MRI edema, EMG, and biopsy).
Polymyositis / immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy:
For: Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness, dysphagia, and inflammatory myopathy on EMG and MRI.
Against: Neither explains the pathognomonic dermatomyositis skin lesions (Gottron’s papules, shawl sign), perifascicular pathology on biopsy, or anti-SAE1/anti-MDA5 antibodies; IMNM typically features markedly elevated CK.
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with secondary myositis:
For: Young Hispanic female, photosensitive rash, positive ANA (1:320 speckled), and muscle weakness.
Against: Gottron’s papules, perifascicular pathology on muscle biopsy, and positive dermatomyositis-specific antibodies (anti-SAE1, anti-MDA5) establish primary dermatomyositis rather than SLE.
Inclusion body myositis (IBM):
For: Muscle weakness with dysphagia and normal or mildly elevated CK.
Against: Typically affects older adults (over 50) with asymmetric distal (finger flexor) and quadriceps weakness, lacks Gottron’s papules/shawl sign and anti-SAE1/anti-MDA5 antibodies, and shows rimmed vacuoles rather than perifascicular pathology.
Myasthenia gravis:
For: Proximal weakness and oropharyngeal dysphagia with normal CK.
Against: Cannot explain Gottron’s papules, shawl sign, elevated aldolase/LDH/transaminases, MRI muscle edema, myopathic EMG, or perifascicular inflammatory myopathy on biopsy.
Polymyositis/IMNM, SLE, IBM, and myasthenia gravis are excluded by the pathognomonic cutaneous findings (Gottron’s papules and shawl sign), perifascicular pathology on muscle biopsy, and positive dermatomyositis-specific autoantibodies (anti-SAE1 and anti-MDA5). I commit to dermatomyositis (anti-SAE1 and anti-MDA5 positive).
Final diagnosis: Dermatomyositis (anti-SAE1 and anti-MDA5 positive)

A synovial haemangioma of the right ankle was resected 11 years earlier. This makes a second vascular synovial lesion in the same limb plausible.
The knee has recurrent atraumatic pain and swelling, which suggests repeated haemarthroses.
X-ray shows epiphyseal overgrowth, a widened intercondylar notch, osteopenia and early degeneration in a 17-year-old. This "haemophilic-like" arthropathy is caused by chronic intra-articular bleeding and hyperaemia during growth.
MRI shows lobulated lesions infiltrating the suprapatellar and Hoffa's fat pads. They are T2/PD-hyperintense, enhance avidly, and are fed by popliteal arterial branches, which means a vascular tumour.
Histology confirms spindle cell haemangioma.
Intra-articular (synovial) spindle cell haemangioma with secondary haemophilic-like arthropathy
Tenosynovial giant cell tumour / pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS)
Haemophilic arthropathy
Synovial sarcoma

Synovial haemangioma
For: prior haemangioma in the same limb, avid enhancement, arterial feeders, fat-pad infiltration, and the arthropathy pattern.
Against: none significant; the histology is diagnostic.
PVNS
For: recurrent swelling, a lobulated synovial mass, and bone remodelling.
Against: no haemosiderin "blooming" or low T2 signal is described, the lesion is T2-hyperintense with arterial feeders, and the histology differs.
Haemophilic arthropathy
For: identical radiographic features.
Against: no bleeding disorder or family history, and a mass lesion is present.
Synovial sarcoma
For: an enhancing periarticular mass in an adolescent.
Against: an 11-year vascular history, an infiltrative fat-pad pattern without aggressive destruction, and benign histology.
Lipoma arborescens
For: fat-pad and suprapatellar location.
Against: the signal is not fat-equivalent and enhancement is avid.
Histology excludes PVNS, sarcoma and lipoma arborescens. The absence of a coagulopathy history and the presence of a vascular mass exclude primary haemophilia. I commit to synovial spindle cell haemangioma causing recurrent haemarthrosis and secondary arthropathy.
Final diagnosis: Intra-articular (synovial) spindle cell haemangioma of the right knee with secondary haemophilic-like arthropathy and muscle atrophy

The patient is a 17-year-old with recurrent, non-traumatic pain, swelling and loss of function in the right knee, plus muscle wasting in the same leg.
He had a biopsy-proven synovial haemangioma of the right ankle 11 years ago, so he has a known tendency to form intra-articular vascular lesions.
The X-ray shows a pattern resembling haemophilic arthropathy: low bone density, epiphyseal overgrowth, a widened intercondylar notch, subchondral sclerosis and joint-space narrowing. These changes come from repeated bleeding into the joint and chronic hyperaemia.
The MRI shows lobulated, coalescent lesions in the suprapatellar and Hoffa's fat pads. They are bright on fat-saturated proton density, intermediate on T1 and enhance strongly with contrast. They are fed by branches of the popliteal artery. These features describe a vascular synovial tumour.
The biopsy confirms spindle cell haemangioma.
Taken together, this is an intra-articular vascular tumour with recurrent bleeding into the joint, causing secondary degenerative arthropathy.
Final diagnosis: Synovial (spindle cell) haemangioma of the right knee with secondary haemophilic-like arthropathy.

He has a relevant past medical history of a biopsy-confirmed synovial haemangioma of the right ankle 11 years earlier.
Radiographs show diminished bone mineralization, epiphyseal overgrowth, intercondylar groove widening, subchondral sclerosis, and joint space narrowing—classic features of hemophilia-like arthropathy caused by recurrent intra-articular bleeding (hemarthrosis).
MRI reveals lobulated, coalescent vascular lesions infiltrating the suprapatellar and Hoffa's fat pads with marked gadolinium enhancement and arterial supply from popliteal branches, along with secondary degenerative changes.

Histopathology (excisional biopsy): Confirmed spindle cell haemangioma, establishing the definitive tissue diagnosis.
MRI of the right knee: Lobulated, nodular, coalescent lesions infiltrating the suprapatellar and Hoffa's fat pads with T1 intermediate signal, PD-FS hyperintensity, marked gadolinium enhancement, and feeding branches from the popliteal artery—hallmarks of a hypervascular synovial/intra-articular vascular neoplasm.
