Conventional synovial haemangioma (cavernous or capillary subtype)
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor / pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS)
Hemophilic arthropathy
Synovial sarcoma
Synovial spindle cell haemangioma of the right knee:
For: Confirmed directly by excisional biopsy histopathology; MRI shows hypervascular, gadolinium-enhancing lobulated lesions supplied by popliteal arterial branches infiltrating the suprapatellar and Hoffa's fat pads; chronic hemarthrosis-like radiographic joint changes (epiphyseal overgrowth, intercondylar notch widening); prior ipsilateral ankle synovial haemangioma.
Against: None; all clinical, imaging, and histologic data align completely.
Conventional synovial haemangioma:
For: Matches the clinical picture, age, MRI hypervascularity, chronic hemarthrosis-type bone changes, and prior history of ankle synovial haemangioma.
Against: Excisional biopsy specifically identified spindle cell haemangioma rather than a conventional cavernous or capillary subtype.
Tenosynovial giant cell tumor / PVNS:
For: Causes monoarticular knee pain, swelling, recurrent hemarthrosis, and lobulated intra-articular synovial masses in young adults.
Against: MRI shows marked hyperintensity on PD-FS and brisk arterial vascularity rather than classic low-signal hemosiderin blooming; definitively refuted by spindle cell haemangioma on histopathology.
Hemophilic arthropathy:
For: Radiographic findings (epiphyseal overgrowth, intercondylar groove widening, subchondral sclerosis, joint space narrowing, osteoporosis) closely mimic hemophilic arthropathy.
Against: No history of a bleeding disorder; MRI demonstrates discrete, enhancing, coalescent vascular masses infiltrating the fat pads; histopathology confirms spindle cell haemangioma.
Synovial sarcoma:
For: Occurs in adolescents/young adults around the knee as a painful, enhancing soft-tissue mass.
Against: Long, recurrent course with chronic bony remodeling and prior benign ipsilateral vascular lesion; ruled out by benign spindle cell haemangioma on biopsy.
Hemophilic arthropathy is excluded by the absence of a coagulopathy and the presence of discrete enhancing intra-articular vascular masses on MRI. PVNS and synovial sarcoma are excluded by both the hypervascular MRI profile and the definitive excisional biopsy. Conventional synovial haemangioma is excluded in favor of the specific histologic subtype proven on pathology. I commit to synovial spindle cell haemangioma of the right knee, which accounts for the hypervascular fat-pad lesions, secondary hemarthrosis-induced arthropathy, and definitive histopathology.
Final diagnosis: Synovial spindle cell haemangioma of the right knee

MRCP: Bilateral intrahepatic and extrahepatic fusiform cystic biliary lesions explicitly matching Todani classification type IVA, which is pathognomonic for choledochal cyst disease.
Abdominal MSCT & hepatobiliary ultrasound: Intra- and extrahepatic biliary ectasia with multiple cystic lesions communicating with the extrahepatic bile duct, plus hepatosplenomegaly and mild splenic vein dilation (secondary biliary/portal changes).
Clinical presentation: 16-year-old female with a 1-year history of intermittent upper abdominal pain, palpable abdominal lump, painless/afebrile jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and tea-colored urine—the classic clinical triad (pain, jaundice, mass) of a choledochal cyst.
Laboratory tests: Direct hyperbilirubinemia (total 9.458 mg/dL, direct 6.635 mg/dL) with elevated transaminases (SGOT, SGPT), confirming obstructive cholestasis.
Choledochal cyst, Todani type IVA
Caroli disease (Todani type V)
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
Obstructive choledocholithiasis with secondary biliary dilatation
Congenital biliary atresia
Choledochal cyst, Todani type IVA:
For: Classic adolescent female presentation with abdominal pain, jaundice, and palpable mass; direct hyperbilirubinemia; US, MSCT, and MRCP all show communicating intrahepatic and extrahepatic fusiform cystic biliary dilatations explicitly classified as Todani type IVA.
Against: None; imaging and clinical findings are completely diagnostic.
Caroli disease (Todani type V):
For: Presents in young patients with intrahepatic cystic biliary dilatation and hepatosplenomegaly.
Against: Caroli disease is restricted to the intrahepatic ducts (Todani type V), whereas this patient has both intrahepatic and extrahepatic cystic lesions (Todani type IVA).
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC):
For: Causes chronic cholestatic jaundice, elevated bilirubin/transaminases, and intra-/extrahepatic biliary abnormalities.
Against: PSC produces multifocal stricturing ("beading") rather than large fusiform intra- and extrahepatic cystic lesions meeting Todani type IVA criteria.
Obstructive choledocholithiasis:
For: Causes intermittent upper abdominal pain, obstructive jaundice, tea-colored urine, and biliary ductal dilatation.
Against: No stones are identified on US, MSCT, or MRCP; ductal dilatation is cystic and fusiform rather than simple cylindrical obstruction, and it does not explain a 1-year palpable mass in a 16-year-old.
Congenital biliary atresia:
For: Causes congenital obstructive jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly.
Against: Presents in the neonatal period with obliteration of the biliary tree, not at age 16 with large dilated intra- and extrahepatic cysts.
Congenital biliary atresia is excluded by age of presentation and patent, dilated ducts. Choledocholithiasis and PSC are excluded by the absence of calculi or multifocal strictures and the presence of discrete cystic biliary dilatations. Caroli disease is excluded because extrahepatic cystic involvement places this squarely in Todani type IVA rather than type V. I commit to Todani type IVA choledochal cyst.
Final diagnosis: Choledochal cyst (Todani type IVA)

A 16-year-old girl has had obstructive (conjugated) jaundice for a year, with dark urine, upper abdominal pain and a palpable mass. This is the classic triad.
Her direct bilirubin is high and her transaminases are raised.
Imaging (MSCT, ultrasound and MRCP) shows fusiform cystic dilatation of both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.
Under the Todani classification, cysts involving both intra- and extrahepatic ducts are type IVA.
The enlarged liver and spleen with splenic vein dilatation suggest early portal hypertension.
Final diagnosis: Choledochal cyst, Todani type IVA.

Type IVA choledochal cyst
For: multiple intrahepatic and extrahepatic cysts in continuity with the bile duct, the classic triad, and a female adolescent.
Against: none.
Caroli disease/syndrome
For: intrahepatic cystic dilatation, and portal hypertension (as in Caroli syndrome).
Against: Caroli disease is limited to intrahepatic ducts, and here there is fusiform extrahepatic dilatation.
Type I with secondary intrahepatic dilatation
For: an extrahepatic fusiform cyst.
Against: the intrahepatic lesions are cystic in their own right, not simple upstream dilatation.

For: cholestasis with intra- and extrahepatic involvement.
Against: cystic ectasia rather than beaded strictures, and her age.
Hydatid cyst or cystadenoma
For: cystic liver lesions.
Against: they communicate with the bile ducts in a ductal pattern, and there is no exposure history.
Extrahepatic involvement excludes Caroli disease. The imaging morphology excludes primary sclerosing cholangitis and parasitic or neoplastic cysts. I commit to Todani type IVA choledochal cyst.
Final diagnosis: Choledochal cyst, Todani type IVA, with obstructive jaundice and possible secondary portal hypertension

CT scan of the right ankle: Posterior malleolus fracture involving 40% of the tibiotalar articular surface with no associated tibial shaft or fibular fractures, confirming an isolated intra-articular posterior malleolar injury.

Against: None; imaging and surgical findings are definitive.
Maisonneuve fracture:
For: Can present with an apparent isolated posterior malleolus fracture on ankle X-rays if the proximal fibula is overlooked.
Against: Physical exam specifically confirmed no tenderness over the fibular head, and CT confirmed no associated fibula fracture.
Trimalleolar or bimalleolar ankle fracture:
For: Common ankle fracture pattern involving the posterior malleolus after a fall on stairs with inability to bear weight.
Against: CT scan explicitly excluded any associated medial malleolar, tibial, or fibular fractures.
Tibial pilon (plafond) fracture:
For: Involves the weight-bearing tibiotalar articular surface after axial loading/fall.
Against: Typically high-energy with comminution and metaphyseal extension; here, X-ray and CT show a clean, obliquely oriented isolated posterior malleolus fracture without tibial shaft/metaphyseal comminution.

For: Physical exam noted swelling and tenderness over the posterior aspect of the medial malleolus.
Against: X-ray and CT confirmed the fracture is in the posterior malleolus with no medial malleolar fracture.

I commit to an isolated posterior malleolus fracture involving 40% of the tibiotalar articular surface.
Final diagnosis: Isolated posterior malleolus fracture

Against: imaging localises the injury to the tibia.
CT and examination exclude associated fractures and Maisonneuve injury. I commit to an isolated posterior malleolus fracture, which was treated successfully with ORIF.
Final diagnosis: Isolated posterior malleolus fracture of the right ankle (about 40% of the articular surface)

A 55-year-old man has a hard, painful, well-demarcated hyperechoic mass in the right lower testicular pole, with microlithiasis on ultrasound. Normal AFP and β-hCG with negative SALL4 and OCT4 argue against a germ cell tumor. Positive vimentin and calretinin with weak CD99 point to a sex cord–stromal tumor. Negative inhibin makes a Leydig cell tumor less likely, and Sertoli cell tumors are often inhibin-negative or variable. Negative D2-40 argues against an adenomatoid tumor or mesothelioma. The hyperechoic, calcified-appearing lesion fits a Sertoli-lineage tumor. The small left epididymal tail lesion was consistent with a benign spermatocele.
Final diagnosis: Sertoli cell tumor of the right testis (with an incidental benign left epididymal spermatocele).

A 55-year-old male presents with a hard, painful, well-demarcated hyperechoic right testicular mass (9 × 11 mm) with testicular microlithiasis and normal serum AFP and β-hCG levels (with only mildly elevated LDH).
Negative immunohistochemistry for SALL4, OCT4, AFP, and D2-40 effectively rules out germ cell tumors (such as seminoma, embryonal carcinoma, and yolk sac tumor) as well as mesothelial/adenomatoid tumors (typically D2-40 positive).
Positivity for vimentin, calretinin, and weak CD99 supports a sex cord-stromal tumor of the testis.
Among testicular sex cord-stromal tumors, Leydig cell tumors are almost universally positive for inhibin, whereas Sertoli cell tumors are frequently inhibin-negative while staining positive for vimentin, calretinin, and CD99.
Final diagnosis: Testicular Sertoli cell tumor

The right testis has a hard, painful 10 × 10 mm mass in the lower pole that is hyperechoic and well demarcated, with microlithiasis, so this is an intratesticular solid lesion. AFP and β-hCG are normal and LDH is only slightly raised, which makes a germ cell tumor less likely. On immunohistochemistry the tumor is vimentin+, calretinin+ and weakly CD99+, which points to a sex cord-stromal tumor. It is SALL4−, OCT4− and AFP−, which argues against seminoma, embryonal carcinoma and yolk sac tumor. It is inhibin−, which argues against Leydig cell tumor, and D2-40−, which argues against adenomatoid tumor and against mesothelial or germ cell origin. The 9 × 5 mm hypoechoic lesion in the left epididymal tail is a separate, benign-appearing finding consistent with a spermatocele. There is no gynecomastia, so no endocrine-active tumor is suggested.
(1) Sertoli cell tumor; (2) Leydig cell tumor; (3) seminoma or other germ cell tumor; (4) adenomatoid tumor; (5) testicular lymphoma.
Sertoli cell tumor. For: the profile is vimentin+, calretinin+ and weakly CD99+, and Sertoli tumors are often inhibin-negative. The germ cell markers and serum markers are negative, and the mass is small and well circumscribed. Against: it is uncommon at age 55, but this is not exclusionary.
Leydig cell tumor. For: it is calretinin+ and vimentin+, and it is the commonest sex cord-stromal tumor in adults. Against: inhibin is negative, whereas Leydig tumors are typically strongly inhibin+. There is also no gynecomastia.
Seminoma or other germ cell tumor. For: the patient is male with a testicular mass, microlithiasis and slightly raised LDH. Against: SALL4 and OCT4 are negative, AFP and β-hCG are normal, and the age is atypical.
Adenomatoid tumor. For: it is calretinin+. Against: it is D2-40 negative, and the lesion is intratesticular rather than paratesticular.
Lymphoma. For: the age is consistent. Against: the vimentin/calretinin/CD99 profile fits, it is a small solitary lesion, and there is no lymphadenopathy.
I exclude germ cell tumors on the negative SALL4/OCT4/AFP staining and normal serum markers. I exclude Leydig cell tumor because it is inhibin-negative, and adenomatoid tumor because it is D2-40 negative. Lymphoma is unsupported. That leaves a sex cord-stromal tumor of Sertoli type, and I commit to it.
Final diagnosis: Sertoli cell tumor of the right testis, with an incidental left epididymal spermatocele.

55-year-old male with a hard, painful 10 × 10 mm right testicular mass: Raises primary concern for a testicular neoplasm; the concurrent left epididymal mass (9 × 5 mm, hypoechoic) is an incidental spermatocele.
Scrotal ultrasound showing a well-demarcated, hyperechoic 9 × 11 mm right intratesticular mass with testicular microlithiasis: Well-demarcated intratesticular lesion; hyperechogenicity is atypical for classic seminoma and can be seen in sex cord-stromal tumors.
Normal AFP and β-hCG with mildly elevated LDH (209 U/L): Argues against non-seminomatous germ cell tumors (yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma) and is non-specific.
Immunohistochemistry positive for vimentin and calretinin, weakly positive for CD99, and negative for SALL4, OCT4, D2-40, inhibin, and AFP: Decisively excludes germ cell tumors (SALL4-, OCT4-, AFP-, D2-40-) and mesothelial lesions (D2-40-), while supporting a sex cord-stromal tumor—specifically one that frequently lacks inhibin expression.
Testicular Sertoli cell tumor (not otherwise specified)
Testicular Leydig cell tumor
Testicular germ cell tumor (e.g., seminoma)
Adenomatoid tumor of the testis
Testicular Sertoli cell tumor:
For: Occurs in middle-aged men; well-demarcated intratesticular mass with normal AFP and β-hCG; IHC profile showing positivity for vimentin, calretinin, and CD99 with negative germ cell markers (SALL4, OCT4, AFP, D2-40); unlike Leydig cell tumors, Sertoli cell tumors are inhibin-negative in roughly half of cases.
Against: Rare tumor (less than 1% of testicular neoplasms); slightly elevated LDH and testicular microlithiasis are non-specific.
Testicular Leydig cell tumor:
For: Most common sex cord-stromal tumor in adults; well-demarcated mass with normal AFP/β-hCG; typically positive for vimentin, calretinin, and CD99.
Against: Negative inhibin strongly argues against Leydig cell tumor (which is inhibin-positive in >95% of cases); absence of gynecomastia or hormonal manifestations; typically hypoechoic rather than hyperechoic on ultrasound.
Testicular germ cell tumor (e.g., seminoma):
For: Most common solid testicular tumor; associated with testicular microlithiasis and mildly elevated LDH; normal AFP and β-hCG can occur in pure seminoma.
Against: Completely excluded by negative SALL4, OCT4, D2-40, and AFP; positive calretinin and vimentin are inconsistent with germ cell origin; older age (55) and hyperechoic ultrasound appearance are less typical for seminoma.
Adenomatoid tumor of the testis:
For: Benign lesion that is strongly positive for calretinin and vimentin; normal serum tumor markers.
Against: Typically paratesticular (epididymal) rather than strictly intratesticular; negative D2-40 argues strongly against mesothelial origin (adenomatoid tumors are characteristically D2-40 positive).
Germ cell tumors are excluded by the negative SALL4, OCT4, D2-40, and AFP staining. Adenomatoid tumor (and malignant mesothelioma) is excluded by negative D2-40 and intratesticular location. Leydig cell tumor is excluded primarily by negative inhibin staining alongside the lack of endocrine signs. Committing to testicular Sertoli cell tumor, as it is the sex cord-stromal neoplasm that best accounts for the vimentin+, calretinin+, weak CD99+, inhibin-negative immunophenotype in a well-demarcated intratesticular mass.
Final diagnosis: Testicular Sertoli cell tumor

An 89-year-old male with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia presents with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, peripheral edema, and notable dysphagia to both solids and liquids with coughing and emesis upon oral intake.
Imaging (chest X-ray, CT, and echocardiogram) demonstrates cardiomegaly and a large pericardial effusion without classic initial signs of cardiac tamponade (no JVD, pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans, or low-voltage QRS), and pericardial fluid cytology is negative for malignancy.
A large pericardial effusion can exert external mass effect on the adjacent esophagus (and left atrium), resulting in mechanical esophageal compression and dysphagia, which explains the combination of heart failure/effusion symptoms and dysphagia that prompted pericardiocentesis.
Final diagnosis: Large pericardial effusion (causing esophageal compression and dysphagia)

The patient has known Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Imaging shows a large pericardial effusion together with bilateral pleural effusions and prominent lymph nodes, which suggests a polyserositis-type process. Pericardial fluid cytology was negative. He had heart-failure-type symptoms with atrial flutter but no tamponade physiology. Other findings are hypoalbuminemia, renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, mild anemia and ecchymoses. Dysphagia with aspiration may be a separate neuromuscular issue given his Charcot-Marie-Tooth syndrome.
(1) pericardial effusion secondary to Waldenström macroglobulinemia; (2) uremic pericarditis; (3) AL amyloid cardiomyopathy related to WM; (4) viral or post-infectious pericarditis; (5) hypoalbuminemic or congestive heart failure effusion.
WM-related effusion. For: the underlying WM, multicavity serous effusions and lymphadenopathy. Against: negative cytology, although this is often insensitive for lymphoplasmacytic disease.
Uremic pericarditis. For: raised BUN/Cr and potassium. Against: the azotemia is modest, and uremia does not explain the pleural effusions or lymph nodes.
AL amyloidosis. For: WM, edema, low albumin, renal dysfunction, atrial arrhythmia and easy bruising. Against: there is no low voltage and no described wall thickening or restrictive pattern on echo.
Viral or post-infectious pericarditis. For: a preceding respiratory infection. Against: no pain, no pericarditic EKG changes, and the lymphadenopathy.
CHF or hypoalbuminemia. For: edema, low albumin and pulmonary congestion. Against: these rarely produce a large pericardial effusion on their own.
Uremia and transudate alone are inadequate to explain the size of the effusion and its multicavity pattern. There is no echo or EKG support for amyloid, and the viral picture is atypical. The most coherent unifying explanation is serosal involvement by the known lymphoproliferative disorder, and I commit to that.
Final diagnosis: Large pericardial effusion (with polyserositis) secondary to Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

An 89-year-old man with Waldenström macroglobulinemia has subacute heart failure symptoms: dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, edema and pulmonary congestion. Imaging shows a moderate-to-large pericardial effusion, bilateral pleural effusions and prominent lymph nodes. There are no clinical or ECG signs of tamponade (no pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans or low voltage), and the effusion was drained by pericardiocentesis. Fluid cytology was negative, but serosal effusions are a recognized, though uncommon, manifestation of WM through lymphoplasmacytic infiltration or cytokine and paraprotein effects. Cytology often misses this. No infectious, uremic-tamponade or other malignant cause is evident. The serositis plus lymphadenopathy best fits WM involvement.
Final diagnosis: Large pericardial effusion secondary to Waldenström macroglobulinemia, with polyserositis and heart failure.

89-year-old male with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, and new-onset dysphagia to both solids and liquids with coughing/emesis: Suggests mechanical esophageal compression in the setting of worsening cardiopulmonary fluid overload.
Large pericardial effusion on CT and echocardiogram, treated with pericardiocentesis: Directly explains cardiomegaly and extrinsic compression of the adjacent esophagus (left atrium/posterior pericardial space).
Negative pericardial fluid cytology for neoplastic cells: Rules out malignant pericardial infiltration from his underlying Waldenström macroglobulinemia or other occult malignancy as a cytologically proven cause.
Absence of JVD, pulsus paradoxus, electrical alternans, low-voltage QRS, and no initial tamponade on echocardiogram: Demonstrates a large, chronic or subacute pericardial effusion presenting atypically with compressive dysphagia rather than classic Beck's triad.
Atrial flutter with variable AV block, pulmonary edema, bilateral pleural effusions, 2+ pitting edema, and renal dysfunction (elevated BUN/Cr, hyperkalemia): Reflects concomitant biventricular/right-sided volume overload and cardiorenal impairment.
Large pericardial effusion causing compressive dysphagia
Decompensated congestive heart failure (with secondary pericardial/pleural effusions)
Malignant pericardial effusion secondary to Waldenström macroglobulinemia
Cardiac amyloidosis (AL amyloidosis secondary to Waldenström macroglobulinemia)
Large pericardial effusion causing compressive dysphagia:
For: Directly documented large pericardial effusion on CT and echo; dysphagia to both solids and liquids with emesis is a recognized compressive complication of large posterior pericardial effusions; required pericardiocentesis with resolution to mild residual effusion.
Against: Dysphagia is an uncommon presentation of pericardial effusion, and no dedicated esophagram or upper endoscopy is reported to directly visualize esophageal indentation.
Decompensated congestive heart failure:
For: Orthopnea, PND, pulmonary edema, bilateral pleural effusions, cardiomegaly, 2+ lower extremity edema, atrial flutter, and prerenal azotemia.
Against: Isolated heart failure does not typically cause acute dysphagia to solids and liquids with emesis, nor does it alone explain the need for pericardiocentesis without a primary large pericardial effusion.
Malignant pericardial effusion secondary to Waldenström macroglobulinemia:
For: Known history of Waldenström macroglobulinemia, prominent lymph nodes on CT, mild anemia, and large pericardial effusion.
Against: Pericardial fluid cytology was explicitly negative for neoplastic cells.
Cardiac amyloidosis:
For: Associated with Waldenström macroglobulinemia; can present with heart failure, pleural/pericardial effusions, arrhythmias (atrial flutter), ecchymosis, and renal dysfunction.
Against: No echocardiographic hallmarks of restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy (e.g., thickened walls, sparkling myocardium), no low-voltage QRS on EKG, and no tissue biopsy confirming amyloid deposition.
Malignant pericardial effusion is excluded by negative pericardial fluid cytology. Cardiac amyloidosis cannot be confirmed and is argued against by the absence of low-voltage QRS or infiltrative findings on echocardiogram. While decompensated heart failure and atrial flutter are concurrent contributors to his dyspnea and edema, they do not account for the prominent mechanical dysphagia to solids and liquids or the indication for pericardiocentesis. Committing to large pericardial effusion causing compressive dysphagia, which unifies the imaging findings, the unusual upper gastrointestinal symptoms, and the therapeutic intervention.
Final diagnosis: Large pericardial effusion causing compressive dysphagia

24-year-old male with a 10-year history of painless, slowly progressive right medial upper eyelid swelling and inferotemporal globe displacement: Indicates a benign, slow-growing anterior superior-medial orbital mass.
Preserved visual acuity (20/20), full extraocular motility, normal optic disc, and no RAPD: Confirms absence of optic nerve compression or invasive malignancy despite the lesion's size (1.95 × 3.16 × 2.62 cm).
MRI showing a well-defined, partially lobulated mass isointense to muscle on T1 with homogeneous contrast enhancement: Consistent with a benign mesenchymal or vascular orbital tumor.
Histopathology showing a monomorphic spindle-cell neoplasm with cigar-shaped nuclei, dispersed calcifications, and no significant mitotic activity or necrosis: Classic morphologic signature of a benign smooth muscle tumor.
Immunohistochemistry positive for SMA and desmin, negative for S100 and CD34: Confirms smooth muscle differentiation and excludes neural and solitary fibrous tumors.
Orbital leiomyoma
Orbital schwannoma
Solitary fibrous tumor of the orbit
Orbital leiomyosarcoma
Orbital leiomyoma:
For: Slow-growing, painless, well-circumscribed orbital mass over 10 years; T1 isointensity to muscle with homogeneous enhancement; monomorphic spindle cells with pathognomonic cigar-shaped nuclei; absence of mitoses or necrosis; positive SMA and desmin; negative S100 and CD34.
Against: Extremely rare in the orbit, though well-documented in the literature.
Orbital schwannoma:
For: Slow-growing, well-defined, painless orbital spindle-cell tumor causing globe displacement without visual loss.
Against: Negative S100 definitively excludes schwannoma; positive desmin and SMA and cigar-shaped nuclei favor smooth muscle over nerve sheath origin.
Solitary fibrous tumor of the orbit:
For: Well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing orbital spindle-cell lesion in young adults.
Against: Negative CD34 strongly argues against solitary fibrous tumor; positive desmin and SMA confirm smooth muscle lineage.
Orbital leiomyosarcoma:
For: Smooth muscle neoplasm positive for SMA and desmin with cigar-shaped nuclei.
Against: 10-year indolent course without pain, invasion, or visual deficits; histopathology shows monomorphic cells with no significant mitotic activity or necrosis, excluding malignancy.
Orbital schwannoma is excluded by negative S100. Solitary fibrous tumor is excluded by negative CD34. Leiomyosarcoma is excluded by the benign histologic features (monomorphic cells, no significant mitotic activity or necrosis) and decade-long indolent clinical course. Committing to orbital leiomyoma based on the definitive smooth muscle morphology and SMA+/desmin+ immunoprofile.
Final diagnosis: Orbital leiomyoma

The patient is a young adult with a 10-year history of slowly progressive, painless proptosis-type displacement and preserved vision, which indicates a slow-growing benign lesion. MRI shows a well-defined lesion in the medial extraconal-to-intraconal orbit that is isointense to muscle on T1 and enhances homogeneously. Histology shows monomorphic spindle cells with cigar-shaped nuclei, no mitoses and no necrosis, which indicates smooth muscle differentiation without malignancy. The tumor is SMA+ and desmin+, confirming myogenic origin, and S100− and CD34−, which excludes nerve sheath tumors and solitary fibrous tumor.
(1) orbital leiomyoma; (2) schwannoma; (3) solitary fibrous tumor; (4) leiomyosarcoma; (5) cavernous venous malformation.
Leiomyoma. For: cigar-shaped nuclei, SMA/desmin positivity, no atypia or mitoses, indolent course, and a well-circumscribed lesion. Against: it is very rare in the orbit.
Schwannoma. For: a slow, well-defined orbital spindle-cell mass. Against: it is S100-negative.
Solitary fibrous tumor. For: an orbital spindle-cell tumor. Against: it is CD34-negative.
Leiomyosarcoma. For: smooth muscle markers. Against: there are no mitoses, necrosis or pleomorphism, and the course is very slow.
Cavernous malformation. For: an enhancing, well-circumscribed lesion. Against: the solid spindle-cell histology.
The immunoprofile excludes schwannoma and solitary fibrous tumor. The absence of mitoses and necrosis excludes leiomyosarcoma, and the histology excludes a vascular malformation. I commit to a benign smooth muscle tumor.
Final diagnosis: Orbital leiomyoma (right medial orbit).

A young man has a very slowly growing, painless, well-circumscribed medial orbital mass. It is extraconal with intraconal extension and displaces the globe down and out. On MRI it is isointense to muscle on T1 and enhances homogeneously. Histology shows a bland spindle-cell tumor with cigar-shaped nuclei and no mitoses or necrosis. SMA and desmin are positive, indicating smooth muscle differentiation. Negative S100 excludes schwannoma and neurofibroma, and negative CD34 excludes solitary fibrous tumor. Bland features favor a benign tumor over leiomyosarcoma.
Final diagnosis: Orbital leiomyoma.

A 24-year-old male presents with a slow-growing, painless right medial upper eyelid mass over 10 years causing inferotemporal globe displacement without visual acuity loss or motility restriction.
MRI shows a well-circumscribed, homogeneously enhancing medial orbital mass extending from the extraconal into the intraconal space.
Histopathology demonstrates a benign monomorphic spindle-cell neoplasm with characteristic cigar-shaped nuclei, dispersed calcifications, and no significant mitotic activity or necrosis.
Immunohistochemistry is positive for smooth muscle markers (SMA and desmin) and negative for S100 (excluding neural tumors like schwannoma) and CD34 (excluding solitary fibrous tumor), confirming a benign smooth muscle tumor of the orbit.
Final diagnosis: Orbital leiomyoma

A woman on warfarin with a supratherapeutic INR has fever and headache. Imaging shows a ring-enhancing, cystic, hemorrhagic lesion with an air-fluid level, meaning a gas-forming organism. CSF shows pleocytosis, high protein and relatively low glucose, which fits a parenchymal abscess. CRP and WBC are low. No contiguous source (sinusitis, dental) or endocardial source was found. Anaerobic culture suggested Clostridium, and molecular sequencing identified the species. A gas-producing Clostridium causing a hemorrhagic abscess most commonly means C. perfringens.
Final diagnosis: Gas-forming hemorrhagic brain abscess caused by Clostridium species (most likely Clostridium perfringens).

A 57-year-old woman on warfarin presents with fever, headache, and mild left-sided hearing loss.
Brain MRI and non-contrast CT reveal a ring-enhancing, cystic, hemorrhagic left hemispheric lesion with an air-fluid level, which is characteristic of a gas-forming brain abscess (with hemorrhage likely exacerbated by therapeutic anticoagulation, INR 2.89).
CSF analysis shows pleocytosis, elevated protein, and hypoglycorrhachia, supporting an intracranial bacterial infection.
Anaerobic culture points to Clostridium species—classic gas-forming anaerobes capable of causing gas-containing brain abscesses—which was definitively confirmed at the species level by molecular sequencing (most commonly Clostridium perfringens).
Final diagnosis: Clostridium brain abscess (gas-forming hemorrhagic brain abscess)

57-year-old woman on warfarin (PT-INR 2.89) presenting with fever, headache, and mild left hearing loss: Raises suspicion for an intracranial infection complicated by hemorrhage.
Non-contrast CT and contrast-enhanced MRI showing a circular, hemorrhagic, cystic lesion with wall enhancement and an air-fluid level in the left hemisphere: Ring/wall enhancement with an intralesional air-fluid level (gas) is classic for a gas-forming brain abscess; anticoagulation explains the hemorrhagic component.
CSF showing pleocytosis (23 cells/μL), elevated protein (125 mg/dL), and hypoglycorrhachia (51 vs. 128 mg/dL): Confirms a bacterial CNS infectious process.
Anaerobic culture suggesting Clostridium spp. and molecular confirmation by shotgun sequencing/rMLST: Establishes a Clostridium species as the causative pathogen of this gas-forming brain abscess.
Clostridial brain abscess (gas-forming hemorrhagic brain abscess due to Clostridium species, e.g., Clostridium perfringens)
Primary intracerebral hemorrhage (warfarin-associated)
Necrotic or hemorrhagic brain tumor (e.g., glioblastoma or metastasis)
Non-clostridial bacterial brain abscess (e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae or Streptococcus spp.)
Clostridial brain abscess:
For: Fever, headache, ring/wall-enhancing cystic lesion with an intralesional air-fluid level (gas production), bacterial-pattern CSF (pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose), anaerobic culture identifying Clostridium spp., and molecular confirmation of the pathogen.
Against: Normal peripheral WBC (5,180/μL) and low CRP (0.04 mg/dL) are atypical for severe bacterial infection; no obvious primary source (no trauma, sinusitis, dental infection, or GI lesion on CT).
Primary intracerebral hemorrhage (warfarin-associated):
For: Therapeutic/supratherapeutic anticoagulation (PT-INR 2.89) and hemorrhagic lesion on CT/MRI.
Against: Cannot explain the intralesional air-fluid level (gas), CSF hypoglycorrhachia with pleocytosis, fever, or isolation of Clostridium spp.
Necrotic or hemorrhagic brain tumor:
For: Cystic, wall-enhancing, hemorrhagic intracranial mass with normal peripheral WBC and CRP.
Against: Air-fluid level (gas) is not a feature of uncomplicated tumors; fever, bacterial CSF profile, and microbiological/molecular confirmation of Clostridium rule this out.
Non-clostridial bacterial brain abscess:
For: Fever, headache, ring-enhancing lesion with gas, and bacterial CSF profile.
Against: Conventional aerobic bacterial cultures were negative, whereas anaerobic culture specifically suggested Clostridium spp.
Primary warfarin-associated hemorrhage and brain tumor are excluded by the gas-forming air-fluid level, infectious CSF profile, and microbiological identification of Clostridium spp. Non-clostridial bacterial abscesses are excluded by negative conventional cultures and anaerobic/molecular identification of Clostridium. Committing to clostridial brain abscess (hemorrhagic, gas-forming brain abscess due to Clostridium species).
Final diagnosis: Clostridial brain abscess (brain abscess due to Clostridium species)

The patient has fever and headache. Imaging shows a ring-enhancing cystic lesion in the left hemisphere with an air-fluid level, which means a gas-forming brain abscess. The lesion is hemorrhagic, and she is anticoagulated on warfarin with an INR of 2.89. CSF shows pleocytosis, high protein and low glucose, consistent with a pyogenic or parameningeal infection. Routine cultures were negative, but anaerobic culture suggested Clostridium spp. and sequencing identified the organism. There is no sinus, dental or cardiac source, and her systemic inflammatory markers are normal.
(1) Clostridial gas-forming brain abscess; (2) brain abscess from another anaerobe or mixed flora; (3) hemorrhagic neoplasm such as a glioblastoma or metastasis; (4) warfarin-associated intracerebral hemorrhage with organization; (5) septic embolism with hemorrhagic infarct.
Clostridial abscess. For: gas in the lesion, anaerobic growth of Clostridium, molecular identification, inflammatory CSF and fever. Against: no obvious portal of entry.
Other anaerobic or mixed abscess. For: gas, ring enhancement and culture-negativity. Against: sequencing pinpointed a single organism.
Hemorrhagic tumor. For: a heterogeneous hemorrhagic cystic mass. Against: gas, fever, CSF picture and microbiology.
Warfarin-associated hemorrhage. For: a supratherapeutic-range INR and hemorrhage. Against: wall enhancement, gas, fever and infected CSF.
Septic embolism. For: her prior embolic stroke. Against: a normal echo and a single lesion.
Gas within the lesion plus the microbiology exclude a bland hemorrhage or tumor. A normal echo makes endocarditis-related emboli unlikely. I commit to a cryptogenic clostridial brain abscess, with hemorrhage aggravated by anticoagulation.
Final diagnosis: Gas-forming hemorrhagic brain abscess caused by a Clostridium species (cryptogenic source; species per sequencing).

An elderly woman fell from standing and was first diagnosed with a left pubic symphysis fracture. She had disproportionate, persistent pain four days later. Repeat X-ray and CT then showed a left femoral neck fracture that was missed or occult on the first films. She was treated with hemiarthroplasty. Concomitant pelvic ring and femoral neck fractures can occur in low-energy falls, and the obvious pelvic fracture can distract from an occult hip fracture.
Final diagnosis: Initially occult (missed) left femoral neck fracture with a concomitant left pubic fracture after a ground-level fall, treated with hemiarthroplasty.

A 68-year-old female sustains a ground-level fall initially diagnosed on plain radiograph as an isolated left pubic symphysis fracture.
Persistent severe pain four days later prompts repeat X-ray and CT imaging, which reveals a previously missed (occult) concurrent left femoral neck fracture alongside mild joint space narrowing.
The diagnosis is further confirmed by definitive surgical management with a left hemiarthroplasty.
Final diagnosis: Concurrent (occult) left femoral neck fracture with left pubic symphysis fracture

The patient is elderly and anticoagulated, with a ground-level fall. A pubic fracture was diagnosed initially, but she still had disproportionate, persistent pain at day 4. Repeat X-ray and CT then revealed a left femoral neck fracture, so the femoral neck fracture was occult or missed on the initial films. Mild joint space narrowing is incidental degenerative change. She was treated with hemiarthroplasty, which is consistent with a displaced or high-risk intracapsular fracture.
(1) occult left femoral neck fracture coexisting with the pubic fracture; (2) isolated pubic rami or symphysis fracture with severe pain; (3) acetabular fracture; (4) intertrochanteric fracture; (5) hip osteoarthritis flare or hematoma on anticoagulation.
Occult femoral neck fracture. For: confirmed on repeat X-ray and CT, with escalating pain after the initial diagnosis. Against: none.
Isolated pubic fracture. For: seen initially. Against: it does not explain the new imaging findings.
Acetabular fracture. For: the fall mechanism. Against: not described on CT.
Intertrochanteric fracture. For: an elderly patient after a fall. Against: the location is the femoral neck.
Osteoarthritis or hematoma. For: joint space narrowing and anticoagulation. Against: the fracture is demonstrated.
Imaging defines the femoral neck fracture and excludes the other options as the main cause. I commit to an initially missed femoral neck fracture alongside the pelvic ring injury.
Final diagnosis: Occult (initially missed) left femoral neck fracture concurrent with a left pubic symphysis fracture, treated with hemiarthroplasty.

68-year-old female with considerable persistent pain 4 days after a ground-level fall initially diagnosed as an isolated left pubic symphysis fracture: Persistent, severe hip/pelvic pain out of proportion to an isolated anterior pelvic ring fracture strongly suggests an occult concurrent hip fracture.
Risk factors for fragility fractures: Age (68), female sex, nicotine use disorder, and chronic hyponatremia (a known independent risk factor for osteoporosis and falls).
Repeat X-ray and CT confirming a concurrent left femoral neck fracture: Establishes the missed second fracture alongside the previously identified left pubic symphysis fracture.
Management with left hemiarthroplasty: Standard surgical treatment confirming a displaced or unstable femoral neck fracture in an older adult.
Concurrent (ipsilateral) left femoral neck fracture and left pubic symphysis fracture
Isolated left pubic symphysis fracture with expected post-traumatic pain
Left acetabular fracture
Osteoarthritis flare of the left hip
Concurrent left femoral neck fracture and left pubic symphysis fracture:
For: Ground-level fall in an older female with fragility fracture risk factors; severe persistent pain 4 days post-injury; directly confirmed on repeat X-ray and CT; definitively treated with left hemiarthroplasty.
Against: Missed on initial X-ray (a known pitfall when an obvious pubic fracture causes satisfaction of search or when the femoral neck fracture is initially nondisplaced).
Isolated left pubic symphysis fracture:
For: Identified on initial X-ray after a ground-level fall.
Against: Excluded by repeat X-ray and CT explicitly demonstrating a concurrent left femoral neck fracture.
Left acetabular fracture:
For: Can accompany pelvic ring injuries and cause severe hip pain after a fall.
Against: Not identified on repeat X-ray or CT, which instead showed a femoral neck fracture and only mild joint space narrowing.
Osteoarthritis flare of the left hip:
For: Mild joint space narrowing noted on repeat imaging.
Against: Mild osteoarthritis does not explain acute severe pain following a fall or require hemiarthroplasty when a confirmed femoral neck fracture is present.
An isolated pubic symphysis fracture, acetabular fracture, and osteoarthritis flare are all excluded by the repeat X-ray and CT demonstrating a distinct left femoral neck fracture. Committing to concurrent left femoral neck fracture and left pubic symphysis fracture (initially missed/occult femoral neck fracture).
Final diagnosis: Concurrent left femoral neck fracture and left pubic symphysis fracture

A 28-year-old primigravida undergoes prenatal ultrasound showing grade 3 fetal echogenic bowel (FEB) at 18 weeks and 3 days gestation, accompanied by progressive fetal bowel dilation reaching 21 mm by nearly 30 weeks.
The primary differential diagnosis for grade 3 FEB includes chromosomal aneuploidy (e.g., trisomy 21), congenital TORCH infections (especially CMV), and cystic fibrosis/meconium ileus (as well as intestinal atresia).
Normal first-trimester screening, low-risk NIPT, normal fetal echocardiogram, and negative maternal TORCH serologies effectively exclude chromosomal aneuploidies and congenital infections.
The combination of persistent grade 3 hyperechogenic bowel and progressive bowel dilation strongly points to inspissated meconium causing intestinal obstruction (meconium ileus), which is classically associated with cystic fibrosis.

Rasmussen encephalitis:
For: Childhood-onset focal seizures, progressive unilateral hemispheric atrophy, and contralateral hemiparesis.
Against: Typically presents in slightly older children (peak 6 years) with insidious, relentlessly progressive epilepsia partialis continua and gradual neurological decline, rather than an acute, permanent hemiparesis immediately following a single prolonged seizure event at age 2.
Childhood arterial ischemic stroke:
For: Acute onset of unilateral hemiparesis, seizures, and subsequent unilateral gliosis/encephalomalacia.
Against: Stroke typically produces focal/territorial encephalomalacia restricted to a specific vascular distribution (e.g., MCA territory), whereas this MRI shows generalized atrophy of the entire right cerebral hemisphere with diffuse subcortical white matter gliosis following prolonged focal seizures.
Sturge-Weber syndrome:
For: Childhood focal seizures, contralateral hemiparesis, developmental delay, and unilateral hemispheric atrophy.
Against: No facial port-wine stain (normal systemic exam) and no leptomeningeal angiomatosis or tram-track cortical calcifications on MRI.
Sturge-Weber syndrome is excluded by the absence of cutaneous or leptomeningeal vascular malformations. Arterial ischemic stroke is less likely because the MRI demonstrates generalized whole-hemisphere atrophy rather than a territorial infarct. Rasmussen encephalitis is excluded by the acute post-ictal onset of permanent hemiparesis at age 2 rather than a subacute progressive inflammatory course. Dyke-Davidoff-Masson syndrome is excluded by the absence of characteristic ipsilateral calvarial thickening and sinus hyperpneumatization. The classic clinical sequence of prolonged unilateral seizures at age 2 causing immediate, permanent contralateral spastic hemiparesis, psychomotor retardation, and diffuse contralateral cerebral hemiatrophy with ipsilateral ventricular dilatation and white matter gliosis commits the diagnosis to Hemiconvulsion-Hemiplegia-Epilepsy (HHE) syndrome.
Final diagnosis: Hemiconvulsion-Hemiplegia-Epilepsy (HHE) syndrome

The patient is a 3-year-old girl with normal early development who experienced prolonged focal seizures affecting the left side at age 2, immediately followed by persistent contralateral spastic left hemiparesis and subsequent psychomotor delay. Brain MRI reveals generalized atrophy of the right cerebral hemisphere with ipsilateral (homolateral) ventricular dilatation and subcortical white matter gliosis. This classic triad of prolonged unilateral seizures in early childhood, permanent contralateral hemiparesis, and unilateral cerebral hemiatrophy is characteristic of hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy (HHE) syndrome.
Final diagnosis: Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy (HHE) syndrome

27-year-old woman with chronic pain, nausea, vomiting, palpable abdominal mass, and recent abdominal trauma with lumbar fracture: Directly links the large abdominal mass to a significant blunt traumatic event.
CT and MRI showing a large (183 x 170 x 73 mm) well-defined peritoneal cystic mass with T1 and T2 hyperintensity and a dark peripheral T2 capsule, with normal liver, spleen, pancreas, and normal multifollicular ovaries: Confirms an extrapancreatic, extra-ovarian peritoneal/mesenteric cystic lesion containing hemorrhagic/blood degradation products (T1/T2 bright with a dark hemosiderin/fibrous rim).
Normal tumor markers and mild anemia: Argues against malignancy and is consistent with prior intralesional hemorrhage.
Histopathology showing a thin-walled cyst with hyalinized hypocellular fibrous tissue, chronic inflammatory infiltrate, capillaries, necrotic debris, and blood clots, with NO epithelial lining and NO neoplastic component: Histologically definitive for a pseudocyst (specifically a non-pancreatic post-traumatic peritoneal/mesenteric pseudocyst).

Against: Relatively rare entity, though every clinical, radiological, and histological feature aligns precisely.

For: Post-traumatic abdominal cystic lesion lacking an epithelial lining on histology.
Against: CT explicitly shows a completely normal pancreas with no pancreatic abnormalities or pancreatitis.

Against: Histopathology reveals only hyalinized hypocellular fibrous tissue, blood clots, and necrotic-hemorrhagic debris, with no caseating granulomas, epithelioid histiocytes, or Langhans giant cells.

For: Large abdomino-pelvic cystic mass in a 27-year-old woman with T1/T2 hyperintensity (mimicking endometrioma).
Against: MRI demonstrated normal multifollicular ovaries (ruling out ovarian origin), tumor markers were normal, and histology lacked any epithelial lining, endometrial glands, or neoplastic cells.
True mesenteric cyst / Lymphangioma:
For: Large well-defined peritoneal/mesenteric cystic mass causing chronic pain, nausea, and vomiting.
Against: True mesenteric cysts and lymphangiomas possess an endothelial or epithelial lining, which is explicitly absent on histopathology.
Ovarian pathology is excluded by normal multifollicular ovaries on MRI, normal tumor markers, and lack of ovarian or endometrial histology. Pancreatic pseudocyst is excluded by a normal pancreas on CT. True mesenteric cysts and lymphangiomas are excluded by the absence of an epithelial or endothelial lining on histopathology. Tuberculous abscess is excluded by the absence of granulomatous inflammation on excision histology. Given the history of recent abdominal trauma with lumbar fracture, hemorrhagic MRI signal with a dark fibrous/hemosiderin rim, and definitive histopathology demonstrating a fibrous-walled, necrotic-hemorrhagic cyst lacking an epithelial lining, the committed diagnosis is Post-traumatic peritoneal/mesenteric pseudocyst.
Final diagnosis: Post-traumatic peritoneal/mesenteric pseudocyst (non-pancreatic abdominal pseudocyst)

The patient is a 27-year-old woman with a history of recent abdominal trauma (with lumbar fracture) presenting with chronic abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and a palpable abdominal mass. Imaging shows a large, well-defined peritoneal cystic mass with T1 and T2 hyperintensity and a dark peripheral T2 rim, consistent with hemorrhagic content and a fibrous/hemosiderin-laden wall. Normal liver, spleen, pancreas, and ovaries exclude pancreatic pseudocyst and ovarian origin, and normal tumor markers argue against malignancy. Histopathology confirms a thin fibrous wall containing chronic inflammation, necrotic debris, and blood clots with no epithelial lining and no neoplastic cells, which is diagnostic of a post-traumatic pseudocyst of the peritoneum/mesentery.
Final diagnosis: Post-traumatic peritoneal pseudocyst

Acute disseminated hemorrhagic, edematous, vesicular, and necrotic skin lesions (predominantly on the head) with oral/nasal mucosal erosions, fever, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and elevated CRP: Classic systemic and cutaneous presentation of severe/bullous/hemorrhagic acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis (Sweet syndrome).
Skin biopsy showing dermal neutrophilic infiltrate with pseudocapsulated yeast-like structures resembling Cryptococcus that stain positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO) and negative for fungal/bacterial stains and cultures: Pathognomonic histopathologic hallmark of cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome (degenerating, vacuolated neutrophils mimicking fungal organisms).
Negative blood, skin, and targeted infectious workup (only non-specific respiratory Candida albicans): Rules out disseminated cryptococcosis and other invasive fungal or bacterial infections.
Pulmonary consolidation, pleural effusion, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and respiratory failure in a patient with p-ANCA/MPO-positive glomerulonephritis on chronic prednisone: Represents extracutaneous (pulmonary) neutrophilic involvement or overlap with underlying ANCA-associated systemic inflammation.
Cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, cryptococcoid variant)
Disseminated cutaneous and pulmonary cryptococcosis
Cutaneous and pulmonary flare of MPO-ANCA-associated vasculitis (microscopic polyangiitis)
Pyoderma gangrenosum (bullous/hemorrhagic variant)
Disseminated histoplasmosis or other deep fungal infection
Cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome:
For: Acute febrile presentation with neutrophilic leukocytosis, elevated CRP, edematous/hemorrhagic/necrotic cutaneous plaques and mucosal erosions, pulmonary involvement (extracutaneous Sweet syndrome), and a definitive skin biopsy showing a dermal neutrophilic infiltrate with Cryptococcus-like pseudocapsulated bodies that are MPO-positive (confirming myeloid/neutrophilic origin) and negative on all fungal stains and cultures.
Against: Mucosal necrosis and severe respiratory failure are atypical for classic mild Sweet syndrome, though well-recognized in severe/bullous/extracutaneous and ANCA-associated variants.
Disseminated cryptococcosis:
For: Immunocompromised host (chronic prednisone, ESRD), disseminated necrotic/hemorrhagic head lesions, pulmonary consolidation, and yeast-like pseudocapsulated structures on routine histology.
Against: Definitively excluded by negative fungal staining, negative skin and blood cultures, negative pathogen serology/PCR, and MPO positivity of the yeast-like bodies (true Cryptococcus does not stain for MPO).
Flare of MPO-ANCA-associated vasculitis (microscopic polyangiitis):
For: Known history of p-ANCA/MPO-positive crescentic glomerulonephritis, positive p-ANCA/MPO titers, low C3, pulmonary infiltrates, hemorrhagic skin lesions, and GI bleeding (melena).
Against: Skin biopsy showed a dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate with cryptococcoid bodies rather than leukocytoclastic vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls; however, Sweet syndrome can occur as a reactive/associated manifestation of ANCA-associated vasculitis.
Bullous/hemorrhagic pyoderma gangrenosum:
For: Neutrophilic dermatosis with hemorrhagic, vesicular, and necrotic cutaneous lesions and systemic inflammation.
Against: Typically presents with rapidly expanding painful ulcers with undermined violaceous borders rather than disseminated edematous head plaques with cryptococcoid bodies on histology.
Disseminated histoplasmosis:
For: Immunosuppression, mucocutaneous erosions, pulmonary consolidation, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and yeast-like bodies on histology.
Against: Excluded by negative fungal stains, cultures, and serology/PCR, as well as MPO positivity of the pseudocapsulated structures.
Disseminated cryptococcosis and histoplasmosis are definitively excluded by negative fungal stains, negative cultures/PCR, and MPO positivity of the yeast-like bodies, proving they are degenerated neutrophils rather than fungi. Pure cutaneous ANCA vasculitis and pyoderma gangrenosum do not account for the specific cryptococcoid neutrophilic histology. Therefore, I commit to cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome.
Final diagnosis: Cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, cryptococcoid variant)

Extracutaneous involvement (pulmonary, mucosal) is consistent with it, and it occurs in the setting of ANCA-associated disease.

Disseminated cutaneous cryptococcosis

Ecthyma gangrenosum or other disseminated bacterial or fungal infection

The patient is a 57-year-old male with p-ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis on chronic steroids who developed acute febrile, disseminated hemorrhagic and necrotic cutaneous lesions, mucosal erosions, pulmonary consolidation with respiratory failure, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and elevated CRP.
Skin biopsy showed a dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate containing pseudocapsulated yeast-like structures closely mimicking Cryptococcus.
Crucially, fungal and bacterial stains and cultures were negative, while the yeast-like bodies stained strongly positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO), proving they are degenerating/vacuolated neutrophils rather than true fungal organisms.
This histopathologic triad (dermal neutrophilic infiltrate, MPO-positive pseudocapsulated Cryptococcus-like bodies, and negative fungal workup) in a febrile patient with hemorrhagic skin lesions and pulmonary involvement is pathognomonic for cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome (an uncommon variant of acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis).
Final diagnosis: Cryptococcoid Sweet syndrome

Six-month history of progressive cough, dyspnea, bilateral lower-lung crackles/wheezes, mild hypoxemia (SpO2 94%, PaO2 65 mmHg, elevated A-a gradient of 41.3 mmHg), and restrictive spirometry with reduced DLCO, indicating a chronic diffuse parenchymal/alveolar filling lung disease.
White, milky bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, which is pathognomonic for alveolar accumulation of lipoproteinaceous surfactant material.
Chest CT showing a diffuse "crazy-paving" pattern (ground-glass opacities with superimposed interlobular septal thickening).
Percutaneous lung biopsy demonstrating alveoli filled with granular, eosinophilic, weakly PAS-positive material.
Borderline-elevated anti-GM-CSF antibodies (4.5 μg/mL; threshold greater than 4 μg/mL), pointing directly to an autoimmune etiology impairing alveolar macrophage surfactant clearance.
Elevated LDH (541 U/L), CEA (30.8 ng/mL), and Cyfra21-1 (14 ng/mL), which are characteristically elevated in alveolar surfactant accumulation, alongside elevated CRP (101.87 mg/L), ESR (74 mm/h), and a positive bacterial culture indicating a superimposed pulmonary bacterial infection.
Autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) complicated by superimposed bacterial infection
Secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (e.g., connective tissue disease-associated or infection-induced)
Pulmonary adenocarcinoma (invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma)
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)
Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD)
Autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) complicated by superimposed bacterial infection: Supported by milky BAL fluid, classic crazy-paving pattern on CT, eosinophilic PAS-positive intra-alveolar material on biopsy, elevated LDH/CEA/Cyfra21-1, borderline-positive anti-GM-CSF antibodies (4.5 μg/mL), lack of clinical response to steroids/antibiotics, and a positive bacterial culture with markedly elevated CRP/ESR (PAP predisposes to opportunistic bacterial infections). Argued against only slightly by the borderline rather than markedly high anti-GM-CSF titer and the weakly positive (rather than strongly positive) PAS staining.
Secondary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis: Supported by the identical histologic/radiologic PAP phenotype, positive ANA (1:80), and positive bacterial culture. Argued against by the presence of anti-GM-CSF antibodies above the diagnostic threshold and the absence of an established underlying hematologic malignancy, toxic inhalation, or overt connective tissue disease.
Pulmonary adenocarcinoma (invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma): Supported by subacute dyspnea, crazy-paving pattern on CT, and elevated CEA (30.8 ng/mL) and Cyfra21-1 (14 ng/mL). Argued against by milky BAL fluid, positive anti-GM-CSF antibodies, and biopsy showing acellular granular eosinophilic PAS-positive material rather than malignant cells.
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP): Supported by hypoxemia, elevated LDH, crazy-paving CT pattern, and frothy/granular intra-alveolar eosinophilic exudate. Argued against by the 6-month chronic course in a host without reported immunodeficiency, milky BAL fluid, anti-GM-CSF antibody positivity, and absence of fungal organisms on biopsy.
Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD): Supported by female sex, chronic restrictive physiology with low DLCO, elevated ESR/CRP, and positive ANA (1:80). Argued against by the low-titer nonspecific ANA without systemic autoimmune features, milky BAL fluid, and biopsy showing intra-alveolar proteinaceous filling rather than interstitial fibrosis or inflammation.
Pulmonary adenocarcinoma is excluded by the absence of malignant cells on biopsy and the pathognomonic milky BAL fluid. PJP is excluded by the chronic 6-month course, lack of immunosuppression, and absence of Pneumocystis on biopsy. CTD-ILD is excluded because the biopsy demonstrates alveolar proteinaceous filling rather than interstitial pneumonitis, and an ANA of 1:80 is nonspecific. Between autoimmune and secondary PAP, the elevated anti-GM-CSF antibody level above the cutoff commits the diagnosis to autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, with the markedly elevated CRP/ESR and positive bacterial culture indicating a concurrent superimposed bacterial lung infection.
Final diagnosis: Autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (complicated by superimposed bacterial infection)

The patient has six months of cough and dyspnea, restrictive physiology with reduced diffusion capacity, and hypoxemia with a widened A-a gradient. The CT shows a classic crazy-paving pattern. BAL fluid was milky white, and biopsy showed granular eosinophilic, PAS-positive material filling the alveoli. Elevated LDH, CEA and Cyfra21-1 are typical surrogate markers of alveolar proteinosis. The borderline-positive anti-GM-CSF antibody supports an autoimmune (or infection-associated secondary) form. A positive bacterial culture from the biopsy in a patient on steroids points to a superimposed opportunistic infection. Nocardia is the classic organism associated with PAP, and it fits the lack of response to the antibiotics used.
Final diagnosis: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (likely autoimmune, GM-CSF antibody–associated) complicated by opportunistic pulmonary infection, most likely Nocardia.

The patient presents with a 6-month history of progressive cough and dyspnea, restrictive ventilatory defect with impaired diffusion capacity, and hypoxemia with a widened A-a gradient. Key diagnostic findings include milky-white bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, a classic "crazy-paving" pattern on chest CT (diffuse ground-glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening), elevated LDH and tumor markers (CEA, Cyfra21-1), and lung biopsy showing granular eosinophilic, PAS-positive material filling the alveolar spaces. These features are pathognomonic for pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP). The borderline-elevated anti-GM-CSF antibody level (>4 μg/mL) supports the autoimmune form of PAP. Additionally, the markedly elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR), partial response to antibiotics/voriconazole, and positive bacterial culture on biopsy suggest a superimposed opportunistic pulmonary infection (such as Nocardia), a well-recognized complication of PAP.
Final diagnosis: Autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (complicated by secondary bacterial pneumonia)

40-year-old female with 3 months of dry cough and exertional dyspnea, right-sided reduced breath sounds, and right-sided cardiac pulsations.
Chest radiograph showing right lung volume loss, ipsilateral tracheal shift, cardiac dextroposition, and tenting of the right hemidiaphragm.
Contrast-enhanced chest CT demonstrating the classic anatomic constellation: anomalous pulmonary venous drainage from the right lung into the infra-diaphragmatic inferior vena cava (IVC), right lung hypoplasia with a hypoplastic right main pulmonary artery, cardiac dextroposition into the small right hemithorax, hyparterial bilobed right bronchus, and anomalous systemic arterial supply from the abdominal aorta to the right lower lobe.
Scimitar syndrome (congenital pulmonary venolobar syndrome)
Bronchopulmonary sequestration (intralobar or extralobar)
Isolated congenital unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia / pulmonary artery agenesis
Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome
Chronic right-sided fibrothorax / post-infectious lung collapse
Scimitar syndrome: Supported by every single imaging finding—anomalous right pulmonary venous drainage to the infra-diaphragmatic IVC, right lung and right pulmonary artery hypoplasia, cardiac dextroposition, bilobed right lung/bronchial anomaly, and systemic arterial supply from the abdominal aorta to the right lower lobe. Nothing argues against it; adult presentation with mild exertional dyspnea and cough is well recognized in partial/adult-type Scimitar syndrome.
Bronchopulmonary sequestration: Supported by anomalous systemic arterial supply from the abdominal aorta to the right lower lobe. Argued against by the presence of global right lung hypoplasia, hypoplastic right main pulmonary artery, cardiac dextroposition, and anomalous pulmonary venous drainage into the infra-diaphragmatic IVC, which define Scimitar syndrome rather than isolated sequestration.
Isolated congenital unilateral pulmonary hypoplasia / pulmonary artery agenesis: Supported by right lung volume loss, ipsilateral tracheal shift, cardiac dextroposition, and hypoplastic right main pulmonary artery. Argued against by the anomalous venous drainage to the infra-diaphragmatic IVC and the systemic arterial supply from the abdominal aorta.
Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome: Supported by unilateral small lung and hypoplastic pulmonary artery in an adult with dyspnea. Argued against by the absence of hyperlucency/air trapping, lack of childhood bronchiolitis history, and the presence of congenital vascular anomalies (anomalous venous drainage to the IVC and systemic aortic arterial supply).
Chronic right-sided fibrothorax / post-infectious lung collapse: Supported by right lung volume loss, ipsilateral mediastinal/tracheal shift, and diaphragmatic tenting. Argued against by no history of TB or prior infection and CT confirmation of congenital pulmonary venous and systemic arterial anomalies.
Chronic fibrothorax and Swyer-James-MacLeod syndrome are excluded because the CT demonstrates congenital vascular and bronchial malformations rather than acquired post-infectious scarring or bronchiolitis obliterans. Isolated pulmonary hypoplasia and isolated bronchopulmonary sequestration are excluded because each accounts for only a subset of the anomalies. The complete triad/constellation of partial anomalous pulmonary venous return to the infra-diaphragmatic IVC, right lung and pulmonary artery hypoplasia with dextroposition, bronchial isomerism, and systemic arterial supply from the abdominal aorta commits definitively to Scimitar syndrome.
Final diagnosis: Scimitar syndrome (congenital pulmonary venolobar syndrome)

Early congenital syphilis: Supported by maternal history of untreated/inadequately treated gestational syphilis, prematurity, high neonatal RPR titer (1:128), and pathognomonic radiographic findings of symmetric metaphyseal radiolucent bands, sclerotic lines, irregular distal radial/ulnar borders, and a proximal femoral metaphyseal osteolytic lesion.
